div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Aristocracy and Wealth.—Lady Crewe and Lady Sybil Grant, the daughters of Lord Rosebery, have both come into a fortune under the will of their great aunt, Miss Lucy Cohen, who belonged to the Rothschild qide of the family. So also has the Hon. Neil Primrose, Lord Rosebery's second son, to enable him to follow a political coreer, like his elder brother Lord Dalmeny. Miss Cehen appears to have been influenced by a desire to equalise matters a little more evenly, which, under our laws gf inheritance, give to the elder sOn the great bulk of the family property. But Lord Rosebery believes in this principle. Not only does it preserve the great estates intact, but he thinks the necessity for tthe younger son to carve out a career for himself is a source of strength to the aristocracy. No doubt he is right, seeing that there is something more creditable in business.or professional career than in a life of idle

pleasuring. - The Setting of two great Stars.—This year sees the retirement into private life of two great stars in the 'musical firmament—Adelina Patti and Mr. Charles Santley. Mr. Santley who was born in Liverpool in 1834, is celebrating the jubilee of his professional career and Patti, who was born in Madrid in 1843, has been almost as long before the public—having made her abut in New York in 1859,—Jenny Lind's operatic successes were then fresh in the public mind, but both Madame Patti and Mr. Santley must possess a right store of reminiscences, knowing as they did, all the great singers of the past half century, such as Sims Reeves, Christine Nilson, Antoinette Stirling, and a host of others. Madame Patti and Mr. Santley have been often associated together in operatic performances on the concert platform, or in oratorios. Verdi, when asked who was the greatest singer in the world replied— La premiere Patti,"" la Seconds Patti, la troisieme Patti," and the retirement of the 'Queen of Song" is not dictated by any decline of her powers. Both she and Mr. Santley are entitled to their well-earned rest but their farewell means a great loss to the music loving world. Colonial Writers and Readers.—Literary tastes as we know, are not the same all the world over, and last year one of the leading women's clubs in London invited stories from lady writers in our Colonial Empire, with a view to encouraging and perhaps discovering unknown talent. Altogether about 300 manuscripts were sent, and these have been judged by a committee of which Mrs. Flora Steel, and Mrs. Annie Swan were members. The stories came from Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, and other parts of the Empire, but those from New Zealand have been awarded the palm, as " unquestionably standing first in excellence.' Some of the best of them are to be published in various magazines and it seems that "the girl's own story book" kind of literature appeals even less to our Colonial sisters than it does to girl readers at home. It is said that "Tom Brown's School Days " is more popular with girls than with boys, and although one may , be Inclined to doubt this, it is true enough that girls have not as a rule any great love for stories written specially for them. Mixed Schooling.—ln •America, the system of educat- ing boys and girls together has been everywhere adopted ilt s not altogether unknown in this country, but so . far it has made little progress, and the results of its introduction next January into St. George's School, Harpenden will therefore be watched with interest. It is claimed in America. that this continuance in school of the conditions of family life, is altogether to the good, and has the effect of Instilling better manners into the boys, and higher ambitions into the girls. That made be the case,although it is contrary to the old idea in this country that a mixed school made the girls rough and hoydenish. Another old-fashioned idea was that whilst the boys must bare a good education, it mattered little about the girls. That notion has to a large extent disappeared, but it will probably be found that the majority of parents still entertain a deep- rooted objection to' having their girls educated at school with other peoples boys. The Christmas Bataars.—Christmas shopping is already in full swing, and it is wise to taki, this in hand at an early date. At many of the Christmas bazaars the system is now adopted of setting out the goods in groups all at one fixed price, and it is just as well to make one's purchases of toys, fancy ebods, and presents generally, before the rush and bustle reaches its worst. Whatever else may fail us, there is no famine in Toyland, and the display is this year more fascinating than ever for the young folks. Every season the array becomes more elaborate and much more is now expected of parents, uncles, and aunts, than in former times, when plain dolls, woolly animals, and other simple toys, satisfied the childish fancy. It is true that most of the old, long-established favourites still remain, but they have become more elaborate and costly, whilst to a great extent the more or less expen- sive mechanical toy has become the fashion. The venerable uncle, in fact can hardly help reflecting upon the marked contrast between now, and the old days when his own youth was nurtured upon hoops and wooden swords. A Desirable Possesion.—A really good lace blouse is s, garment we should strive to possess, as it can be made to blend any skirt, does not date as coloured blouses have a habit of doing, and moreover returns from a visit to the cleaners looking perfectly new. The blend- 'tug process is best accomplished by means of "braces" which must be of the same fabric as the skirts with which they are to be worn, or built up of the same
ied— 1

trimmings as thoie appearing upon the, skirt. In velvet these "braces" look particularly well, especially when they are cut to widen out upop the shoulders, and ar,e latticed across the front with narrow velvet ribbon. Trains fashionable.—The long sweeping skirt for out- door wear is happily gone past recall, but at the moment all indoor gowns are trained. The afternoon frock has its funny little wisp-like tail ; dinner toilettes sweep all round and at the ba,tk lengthen out into quite moderate trains, while the ankle-length dance dress has given place to the one which barely escapes the floor. Undoubtedly the long afternoon dress is very graceful and most desirable, provided it can be kept for the house. The girl or woman who has, howaver, to com- bine the house and walking skirt, should have it built for the latter purpose and ignore Fashion's latest whim. About Veils.—Pale blue tulle, spotted with black chenille is the leading veil, and certainly it is much more flattering to the generality of complexions, than the so-called" beauty ' veils, which are of a pinkish hue, and particularly trying. The fashionable woman gathers up her veil loosely behind, and dispenses with the one time modish" fall." This is quite as well con- sidering the milliners are massing the whole of the trimmings at the back of our hats. To the uninitiated it would appear that the up-to-date woman had put on her hat "wrong ways abouti' and a long veil depending from the back of these top-heavy arrangements would certainly not improve matters. New and Inexpensive Jewellery.—The new Wediwood jewellery, formed of tiny plaques, upon which little white figures—designed by Flaxman—stand out on the most exquisite pale blue, pale pink, or pale green back- grounds, promises to be much in request among Christ- mas present seekers. These little plaques set off by blister pearls, and held t )gether by slender chains, make the most charming necklets, while single speci- mens are mounted as hat pins, cuff-links, and buttons. With the pale pastel shades so much in evidence, the new Wedgwood jewellery looks particularly well. A Useful Christmas Gift.—A six yard 521 n. wide dress length of the new Wyluyrwell Fabric (6s. 6d.) would make a delightful Christmas gift, and doubtless we shall not be slow to take advantage of Messrs. Lutas Leathley's offer to forward from Armley,Leeds, carriage paid, this particular bargain. This firms selections of patterns which are sent post free, and need not be returned are wonderful, ranging as they do from the thickest and most useful materials, down to the most beautiful and airy fairy of ball fabrics. MAD GE.

The story related to a "West Bromwich Chronicle" reporter by Mrs. Eliza Potter, of 18, Long-square, Hill Top, West Bromwich, of how Bile Beans cured her of ulcerated stomach, speaks for itself. Said Mrs. Potter: —" In November, 1903, I became very seriously ill. I was so weak and in such great pain for many weeks that I gave myself up for death. I could not keep anything on my stomach, and was always in pain. I became so • weak and worn that I was like a shadow. "I tried several different doctors and went to a hospital, and they all said that I had an ulcerated stomach but all the medicines they gave me did me no good, and I was more dead than alive. I could not touch bread, or any solid food, and had to live on milk and eggs. I was two-double ' with pain and could not bold myself straight. Every scrap of food I took caused me terrible pain. "At last I was induced to try Bile Beans. Before I had finished the first box I went for A short walk. On my return I was able to eat the first bit of solid food I bad taken for five months, and I bad no -pain after it. I continued taking Bile Beans, and very soon I was able to eat without fear of pain, and to retain food on my stomach. Gradually my strength returned, until I was strong and vigorous again. Two years have gone by since Bile Beans cured me, and I have not again been troubled with my stomach." Of all chemists at Is. lid. or 2s. 9d. per box. Bile Beans are not sold loose or out of jars.

CONIMF.R.CIAL FATLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazetth," the total number of Commercial failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, November 30th, was 172, viz. : New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 96 ; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 76. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 116 ; Deeds of Arrangement, 75—total 191; being a decrease of 19. The total num- ber of Commercit.l Failures recorded during the 48 weeks of the present year is 7,770 ; the total number rccorded in the corresponding 48 weeks of last year was 8,331, showing a decrease of 561.

div.head: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
div.p: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
EALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
BY ALICE MAUD MEADOWS, Author of "One Life Between," "A Million ot Money," "The Extreme Penalty," "For Love of s Lady," "I Charge You Both,' dca.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: It is the wedding eve of John Brandon, a well-to-do country gentleman, and Celia Verde, daughter of Lady Caroline Verde. Celia had 131,n engaged to John:s brother Dick, a wild and rockless young man, supposed to have died al*oad.' .Celia admits that she loved her old' sweetheart better than the new— in fact, that she does net love John at all. He, however, adoring her. p:Anises himself that he wilt win leer love after marriage. Then all is changed by the sudden 'reappearance of Dick, who I meets his brother as he is going homewards. No ' other person has seen the wanderer except Lady . Caroline's maid, who takes him for a ghost. John Brandon lets his brother in by the library window, unseen by his servants. Dick laughs at the idea of I JOhn marrying Cilia, who, he is certain, still loves ' himself. His careless taunts excite, John to fury, and he strikes his brother violently on the head with a ruler, intending only .to disable him until after the. wedding takes place. ,To his horror, however, the signs of death are manifest. With quiet resolution he places the body in a large safe. At that moment the police, arrive at the house in search of a convict who has just escaped from a neighbouring prison. They insist on examining the house, as the: fugitive has been traced in that direction. Finally they open the safe. John Brandon is in an agony of fear. The safe is empty!

div.head: / CHAPTER VIII. "No. 27."
div.p: / CHAPTER VIII. "No. 27."

John heard the front door closed, then once more his manservant came to him. Believing in his master absolutely as he did, he yet could not help glancing somewhat curiously at the open safe. There was no doubt that the-yotrng man b.ad been in mortal fear, but, whatever the reason, Robert was certain it was not that suggested by Warder Clark.
"Can I do anything for jou, sir?" he asked. "Nothing—nothing, thank you, Robert," he answered.

"This has been an upsetting evening, sir ? " "Very upsetting. I'm sorry you have all had your night's rest disturbed. Get to bed now, and to sleep, as quickly as you can." "You'll be sitting up a little later, sir?" "Yes." John Brandon spoke somewhat im- patiently. " Good-n ight. " The mun went from the room, closing the door after him.

John listened, heard his footsteps die away in the distance, then he rose. He remembered quite well that be had locked the safe; it would have been madness not to have done so. With an effort he remembered also where he had put the keys; he opened the desk and looked. Yes, they were there—there just as he had left them. Then how, in the name of wonder, had this thing happened? He sat down and pressed his hands to his ' temples'. Had it been a dream? He had heard of such things being so vivid that the dream was believed in and -looked upon as a reality. Was it possible he had not met and walked with his brother? Neither quarrelled with, nor killed him? The empty safe seemed to say that was so, and yet— His eyes fell upon the handkerchief, and he took it up. Dick had always been ridiculously particular about such things, always a bit of a woman where linen was concerned. He turned the bit of cambric about in his hands, then his eyes fell upon the initials "D. 8. It hacl not been a dream—Dick had been there. Where was he now?

He had pushed the door of the safe to. Now he rose and opened it again, looking in eagerly. On one side there was a dark mark—he knew instinctively it was blood—that was all. He closed the door once more.

"It's enough to drive a man mad ! " he said, half-aloud. "And to-morrow will be my wedding- day! To-morrow "—he looked at the clock—" no— to-day ! " "It's no good thinking of it," he said to himself. "It's a mystery; I cannot understand it. I locked a dead man in my safe • I put the keys away. The safe has been opened—the dead man is gone ; I must dismiss the whole thing from my mind; if Ido not, I shall be more fit for a lunatic asylum than to be the husband of a sweet young girl." His crime troubled him not at all. Perhaps he was too utterly tired, worn out, to be troubled by anything. He,moved towards the door. His hand was on the electric switeh, when there came a faint tap at the window. He paused, his nerves in such a state of tension that he trembled again, and yet it was nothing but the branch of a tree stirred by the wind striking the glass. He made another step towards the door; the tapping was repeated, more loudly, more per- sistently this time. He .hesitated, crossed the room, and stood by the French window. . . .
The tapping came again, then a voice, soft bui very penetrating: "Let me in, quietly; turn down the light first, quickly—there's no time to be lost—your own safety depends upon it." •He hesitated.

"Your life," the voice said, "your love— posOpssion of the woman yoil love ! Open quickly ! Hang you, man, don't keep me waiting!" John Brandon crossed the room, switched off the light, returned to the windows shot back the bolts, and opened it. The moon was again clouded, but a certain amount of light remained—enough for John to see that a man stood before him, a man whose clothes were decorated with broad arrows; the escaped convict, no doubt. He stepped in and closed the window after him.

"Don't turn up the light again," he said, "they're still watching from a distance; let them think you've gone to bed. You know who I am, of course?" "The man from Dartmoor, the convict. I can't harbour you; you can't stop here!" The man moved further into the room; sat down.

"Oh, I think yGU can; „I think you he answered. "When you'vd heard all, I'm sure you will; you've no other alternative. I've done you a good turn to-night—you'll return it. If you don't, my friend, I'm afraid your ultimate destination will be a very unpleasant one. Murder is a crime upon which the law does not smile!" "What—what do you mean ? " John Brandon's white lips could hardly articulate the words. He shut the French window quickly, but softly, then he almost collapsed into a chair. He had gone through almost as much as he could bear this evening, and now a convict knew of his crime, the victim of which had disappeared in so aartling a way! The man laughed, sat down, helped himself to brandy-and-soda, then turned again to John Brandon. •

"Oh, come now," he said, in a perfectly refined tone, "you know very well what I mean, though I can quite understand you can't imagine how I know anything of your private affairs ; that's easily explained. I escaped to-night from Dartmoor, and made my way across the country as quickly as possible. My one thought was to reach a house where I could steal a suit of clothes. I'd no idea of hiding for days and days, to be hunted like a wild beast, and caught again at last, as I must be in these things. Once arrayed in ordinary clothes, I felt I should be absolutely safe. Money has been lying hidden for me in a spot I know of for over a year; that money is now in my pocket, the one pocket they give us convicts. It was put there for me by a friend; the information leaked through even the prison walls. This wig I am wearing—you didn't know it was a wig, did you ?—was hidden in the same place. In an ordinary suit no one could recognise me ; I meant to get that suit somewhere —here, as it turned out. Chance, fate, call it whatever you like, led me here. I watched the house, waiting for the lights to be turned out, listening for the booming of the guns, which sooner or later was sure to tell me my flight had been discovered. They were longer finding out than I expected. I thanked Heaven for it—oh, yes, I did, though I hadn't prayed for years. We convicts get plenty of church, plenty of parson: but one's spirit isn't tuned to thankful- ness or hymns of praise in Dartmoor. And then you and your brother came along." John Brandon gripped the arms of his chair, across the utter pallor of his face a leaden shadow stole.
"You were not talking much," the man went on. "but what you said I heard. It seemed to

me sensation, tragedy were in the sir. I gathered the nucleus of the situation at once: both of you loved one woman, both of you had at different times been engaged to her; one of you only had she loved—your brother—who was supposed to have died abroad. You were to, marry her on the morrow to-day. Could anything, I asked myself, more lend itself to the brand of Cain? I watched you into the house; I stole up to the window; I listened. Now and then, through the blind being slightly'open one side, I could see. You _quarrelled, as it was inevitable you must; you fought, as all male creatures will fight for the thOlig feminine that is loved. You in your passion killed your brother. I saw it all. Whether or no I could have stopped it I do not know. I did not think it would come to murder."

John Brandon's eyes travelled round to the safe, mutely asking an explanation. His parched tongue tried to moisten his dry lips. He could not have spoken had he tried. "You thought yolar brother stunned," the man went on; "you did not think him dead. You soon found out your mistake, and then came the question, What should Feu do with him ? Where hide him?"

Again John's eye turned towards the safe, the empty safe, in which he had hidden his brother. "It is difficult to understand, isn't it ? " the eonvict asked. "It savours of magic, but the explanation is quite simple. I had seen all that had happened, and in the meantime I had also heard the booming of the guns, which told the world—or, at all events, as many as could hear-- that a prisoner had escaped. Two things occurred to me. If by any chance the prison officials should trace me in the direction of your residence, which was very likely, the house would be searched, the safe might possibly be looked into, and quite innocently I should have been the means of betraying a fellow-sinner, who, whatever his crime was against another, had done me no harm. I should, as it were, hand him over to the hangman, or, at least, to a prison life." "The second thing that occurred to me was this—you were in my power, for my own benefit I could make you my tool. "I was just going to knock at the window, when you turned out the lights and went from the room.

"I had seen where you had hidden the keys of the safe. Now that you had gone from the room a new idea occurred to me. I wanted a suit of clothes; the murdered man—sorry to use the word—dead man, then, had on him everything I wanted. Was it possible to possess myself of the body, and make a change? He would never be mistaken for me, I knew, when the full light of day was, turned upon him; but, dressed in my clothes, he might be for a little while, until they reached the prison. It might give me an hour more. Any way, the clothes were almost vital to my safety. I saw at once, of course, that if I were caught with them on me, I might be suspected of the murder. I must risk that, and I would not wear them longer than was necessary. I. would get rid of them, sink them in some river. And I did not forget, you may be sure, that so long as I held my tongue you would of necessity be my banker for the rest of my life! 1 "I tried the door. I knew in a iniute there were bolts as well as a snap lock. I had no time and no tools with which to tackle them. A glance upward showed me a fanlight; with them I have never had the slightest difficulty. To cut what to you may seem a very long, story short, I made my way in, possessed myself of the keys, opened the safe, and five minutes - after had carried the dead man out into the open, pulling the door, which locked itself, after me. The keys, without locking the safe, I threw into the drawer." John Brandon did not speak. The mystery of the disappearance from the safe was now explained. The dead man had been taken from the house by this convict- in order that he might dress himself in his clothes. Why, then, had he not done so?

"I carried my burden some distance," the man went on, "and laid it down in a ditch, a perfectly dry ditch, in which I should not at all have minded a sleep myself. I still heard the guns going. I had almost become accustomed to them now. I had half unfastened my coat when I heard voices and footsteps near me. I had to leave the clothes I so much wanted and steal away in the semi-darkness. As it turned out I might have stayed where I was. They did not find the dead man, well hidden as he washy long rush grass; they would not have found me. When the place seemed pretty clear of them I tried to steal back, but could not find where I had laid my burden. I could have sworn I returned to the spot, but I was mistaken—other- wise I should not have come to you to-night. I should have left you in peace, or "—he smiled grimly—"in as much peace as you can expect to enjoy. With an effort John Brandon pulled himself together. He saw all the horror of the situation. He was in the power, absolutely in the power, of this convict for the future. In a way he would, or at all events could, rule his life—ask of him what he would, with the knowledge that the man whose secret he held dare not refuse him.
"And you want—what ?" he asked. "Clothes to get away n, I suppose? I have no alternative, of course, but to give them to you. Wait quietly here, I will fetch you. a suit."

- The convict stopped him with a gesture. "An hour or two ago," be said, "to get a suit of clothes in exchange for these was the greatest good thing I could imagine. Things, however, have changed a little since then. I want some- thing more. The prison authorities, the police, will scour the country for a man who is running away; every railway station, every port will be watched. In London they will hunt for use as the hounds hunt a fox. I think I could have dodged them, but I'm not sure. The man who is running away is always at a disadvantage. Now, how- ever, happily, most happily, there is no need to do anything of the sort. I shall not run away, I shall 'stay here." John Brandon sat suddenly up in his chair, as though he had been electrified. "Stay here;?" he repeated. "You—you must be mad!" Once more the man helped himself to brandy- and-soda. "Not half so mad as you, if you refuse," he answered. "I admit it's an unpleasant thing for you to be forced to do, but I'll make it as little unpleasant as possible. You've probably gathered from my manner of speech that by birth and education I am what is called a gentleman. lain not going to say I was not guilty of the crime for which I was imprisona I was, hut I am not in the least likely to put myself again within the power of the law, excepting, of course, ,so far as you are concerned. I have, lam aware, made myself an accessory after the fact. I am well informed upon most subjects. I can talk well. I could pass in your set as your equal. This .is what I want you to do, what—l'm sorry to seem impolite—you must do. To-morrow, to-day I should say, will, with my permission, be your wedding-day. No doubt you have friends coming down for the occasion, friends who will come here; some of them fairly early, perhaps. Take sae up to your own room now, give me a shake- down there. Take my clothes and lock them up safely somewhere; not in the safe—l mistrust safes. ,You must have, several new suits of clothes, some that your man even, perhaps, has not seen. You have, no doubt, more than one frock-coat.. We are very much of the same height and build. I could wear your clothes and look perfectly well in them. You must put ready for me everything a gentleman would require in which to attend a wedding. "Early in the morning before the servants are about, with just enough noise to be heard, with- out unduly disturbing anyone, you must go down to the front door, open it, and feign to let some- one in. After that, all is plain sailing. You will introduce me to everyone as your old friend, Fred White, or any name you like, who, hearing you were to be married, has turned up un- expectedly to be present at the wedding. Among your guests I shall be quite safe; no one will look for No. 27 there. For a few days after you have gone away I will stay on here, keeping quiet, lying low. Directly I see a chance of getting away I will go. For your own sake and for mine, I hope you will not find me here when you return. Look out and see if the coast's clear. I I don't feel at ease in the clothes provided by his Majesty's Government." They had been talking in the dark, in low, hushed voices. Only dimly could they make out the ou:line of each other's forms. Neither could see the face of the other, nor tell the secret workings of the other's heart. And in the heart of John Brandon against this man who knew his secret, his sin, this man who —for his own sake certainly—had saved him I from horrors unutterable, there Was terrible anger. Once to-night he had taken a life, once more before his eyes, even in the deep darkness, there was a blood-red mist. Had he dared hi would have killed for the second tiins—and not for his own sake.

This man, so long as he lived, was hie master, had the whip hand of him, the curb rein. Hs dare not defy him—dare he kill him? Ones before to-night he had discovered what many a murderer has, that it is easier to slay than to hide. And yet to accede to this man's request would be monstrous.

Monstrous, because, upstairs, sleeping, no doubt, while a tragedy had been enacted, the beautiful, peaceful sleep of the young, lay a sister, next to Celia Verde the dearest creature in the whole wide world to John Brandon. Could he be so base as to bring this man into close companion- ship with her? The thins was impossible. "I will rig you out in clothes," he said, a tense note in his voice, "I will give you what money you like, but you must go. I can't keep you here. I have another, not only myself, to consider."

'I shall not hurt that other—a woman I suppose, a sister ? You shall have nothing— nothing to complain of. But that's my alterna- tive—either you fall in with my wishes, or I give you up to justice. It will mean prison for me again, I know, but no prison will keep me In. long. As for you, the thought of to-day is less dear to you than one might have imagined if you hesitate." He heard John Brandon draw his breath very deeply, then he knew that he rose, moved stealthily: In a minute the hand of the convict was on the electric switch, the room a blaze of light. The two men looked at one another. There was murder in the eyes of one. The convict moved back a step. "What, not satisfied ?" he said. "Isn't one soul sent to its last account with all its imper- fections on its head enough responsibility for one twenty-four hours ? Any way, I've no intention of being murdered, none whatever. Shall we go upstairs now, my friend ?." The wild look faded from John Brandon's eyes. He made a gesture of assent. The convict spoke in a whisper. "Go on, I'll follow you; softly--softly. I'll see to the light. Oh, to sleep and to wake a free man—how good that will be!"

div.head: CHAPTER IX. YERNON:SALISBURY.
div.p: CHAPTER IX. YERNON:SALISBURY.

Quite early in the morning John Brandon rose, went downstairs, made a good deal of noise in opening the front door, spoke, apparently, to someone who was there, though no one was visible, then, still talking, went back to his room and slammed the door to.

At half-past seven he rang his bell and his man appeared. John Brandon was still in bed, but from the bath-room, which opened from it, came the sound of merry whistling and tho' splashing of water. John looked at his man sleepily, his arms above his head. "Sorry to rouse yeti so early after the upset of last night," he said, "but 1 want you to get us some tea as quickly as possible. Don't be long" —he stifled a yawn—"there's a good fellow." The man looked towards the bath-room, his expression a very strange one.

4 L's ! " he repeated. - John Brandon stared at him for a minute, then laughed. "How stupid of me!" he said. "I took it for granted that you knew Mr. Vernon Salisbury turned up at half-past five this morning; threw stones up at my window. I went down and let him in—l wonder you did not hear me; he's tubbing now, but he'll be as glad of a cup of tea as I shall. I'd no idea he was even in England; it seems he only returned last night, heard of my approaching wedding, and determined to be present. We'll have a little bread and butter too, please." "Very good, sir," the man answered, and backed out of the room.

He was not surprised; he was utterly unsus- picious. He had not been with John 'Brandon very long—certainly not long enough to know all his friends, of whoM his master had a great many; it was quite a custom, too, for them to throw .stones at his window to awaken him, sometimes that he might join them in an early walk or ride.

He went quickly downstairs. John Brandon waited until he could no longer hear his foot- steps, then called out: "Can you conic in here?" "Half a minute, my dear Jack," a man's voice answered, and John winced at the familiarity. "A tub like this is something of a hatury. I don't mean to say that my last hotel "—there was a laugh in his voice—"lVlLS deficient in that respect; still, they didn't supply us with scented soap, or other little luxuries, which really make a bath worth taking. I can quite see that I shall be very comfortable and happy here." John Brandon smothered a groan. If wishing could have made the man dead, ho most certainly would by now have put off this mortal coil; unfortunately for the prospective bridegroom, it does not.

He realised that. he was absolutely in the man's power; that to any tune piped he must dance; that in every way he had the whip hand of him. The man was a convict, certainly, and stood in fear, no doubt, to a certain extent, of being given up to justice ; but his crime was not one that merited death. The greater criminal was afraid, naturally afraid, of the lesser. And afraid not only of h own crime being disclosed by this mail, but in terror that the police, more sharp than us No. 27 thought them, might penetrate 1.4 disguise, re-capture him, and punish the man who had harboured him. Even the joyousness of the day could not chase away the gloom and horror that had fallen upon John Brandon. He tried to shake it off, but failed. He had spent a restless, sleepless night trying to think what was best to be done under the circum- stances. This man proposed to stay on in his home after he had gone for his honeymoon—the thing was impossible. Every day there must be danger of detection ; there was also his eister, Olive, to be considered. She was young, beautiful, innocent almost entirely of the world, its ways, and wickedness. If he introduced the convict as an old friend, she would extend to him at once an almost boyish friendliness, utterly without embarrass- ment or restraint ; she would become a good comrade at once, and could such a man—a felon --be expected to respect such friendliness ? If the man insisted upon staying, she must be sent away. Yet that would look suspicious at once. . His thoughts stopped abruptly, a soft step sounded on the carpet, time convict had entered the room.

John Brandon could not help a start of surprise; the man looked fresh as paint, fit as a fiddle. He had dressed himself in morning attire, excepting so far as a velvet smoking jacket was concerned; the wig which covered his closely cropped hair suited him to perfection, and to John Brandon seemed absolutely undetectable. His eyes and lips were laughing as though he thought the whole thing a good joke. He was more than commonly handsome, tall, splendidly set up. His days spent in prison, the plain yet wholesome food, the outdoor work which had been his fortunate chance, compulsory teetotalism, and long hours of rest had probably made a better man of him than ever ho had been before in his life. He looked' like a young athlete. There was not a woman in ithe world who would not have been attracted by his hand- some personality.

"Good-morning, Jack," he said, carelessly, and flung himself into a chair. "I heard my name—Vernon Salisbury. Don't know that I wouldn't have preferred a less high-flown one, but, after all, what's in a name I Would you like to know my real one? You'll remember

close at once, ir t tell it you. John Brandon made a gesture of dissent. "Not for the world!" he said. "I want to know nothing about you; you've forced yourself upon me, but there is no reason, so far as I know, why I should be informed what particular villainy brought you within the walls of Dartmoor."

Vernon Salisbury, as John. Brandon had named him, stared at his companion for a minute or two, then burst out laughing. "Well, I'm sure!" he said, quite cheerfully. "If you don't beat anything I ever knew. Why, man, whatever I have done, I don't deserve to have the hangman's rope dangling round my neck, and you do! Doubly so, since the poor fellow you've sent to his last account, with all his imperfections on his head, happens to be your brother! Don't try to do the virtuous individual with me, it won't wash. We'll waive my past peccadilloes ; after all, they are not interesting. In the language of the late some- body or other, we'll cut the cackle and get to the 'oases—you're going to make things as soft for me as possible. I'd better be your old friend— your dear old friend just returned from Australia."

Re laughed again as he spoke then both men were silent. Robert could be heard coming up the stairs, a clinking of china served to tell he was bringing the tea. Vernon Salisbury blid risen, and was wandering in a familiar manner about the room as the., man entered.

"What a conservative old chap you are, Jack," he said. "Everything just as it was wlken I left England; every picture, every ornament" in the same place. Most folk alter everything every spring-cleaning; variety and change, they say, is the secret of health. You've no such notions, you dear old slowcoach. Ah, tea! Now, if I'd had Aladdiif s ring or Aladdin's lamp, I should have rubbed it and commanded the slave who would have made his appearance, probably through a mysterious trap-door, to bring me a cup of the best Bohea." Robert looked at him and laughed. "It's better than Bohea, sir," he said • "it's a mixture of my own. A pound of the very best black, two ounces of orange Pekoe, and Itn ounoe of green—it's a mixture fit for the gods. I've "—he turned to his master—"made you a bit of a sandwich, sir. I thought it might -be agreeable to you after the turmoil of last night." John Brandon nodded. Robert set the tray down on a table, poured out the tea, and handed it, first to the visitor, then to his master. When he had also provided them with sandwiches, he let his tongue run freely. "Mr. John," he said, 'I had a few words with a police-constable who seemed patrolling about here. They've not caught the convict yet, it seems; they've been on two or three false scents. Well, as far as I am concerned, I hope they won't catch him; he seems the darned 'cutest— begging your pardon, Mr. John—prisoner, they have ever had; and, after all, his offence was only one against the law, not against life, or anything really serious. Gentleman Jim, it seems, they felt bound to ball him, even in a penal prison. I can't help but take off my hat to one who claims such a distinctive title under the most adverse circumstances."

Vernon Salisbursy burst out laughing. "You rogue !" he said. "I don't believe you'd give him up to justice even if you came across him Jack, I think we ought to warn the police that the convict from Dartmoor has a sympathiser in your household. We woulin't mention names, of course; but, after all, justice is justice, and the law ought to take its course—that's if it can. Sometimes advdrse circumstances prevent." Robert grinned. "I believe you're joking, sir," he said. 'I believe you'd give the poor fellow a hand. I'm not one as is against the punishment of crime—hang the murderer, I say; black-list the drunkard; cat-o'-nine-tails the bully; punish the thief—but I must say I do feel for those who are suffering penal servitude; you can't imagine what it is, sir. There's many a prisoner who succumbed to a sudden temptation; who was tempted and fell almost, one might say, before he really knew what he was doing. After they are sentenced and punished, there are men who would be willing to do their duty in that walk in whieh fate and their own weakness has seen fit to plant them; who'd work out their five or ten years peaceable enough if only they were treated as humans. But think what it must be, sir, to work with armed men standing round you; to be afraid to throw up your arms for pure exhilaration of spirit engendered by the fresh air,which Heaven sends even to convicts working in the quarries; to take a bounding step, but a bullet whizzes through you! It's not the work or the confinement that hurts them; it's the repression. After all, they are men—it must be painful to live the life of an automatic figure. I don't say I'd aid and abet a convict—l wouldn't harbour one—but if I see a man decorated with the broad arrows pass me by, I'd shut my eyes, and if anyone interrogated me with regard tc him, I should take the liberty .of having seen nothing. It's my belief and hope the man got safe away." "And mine too," Vernon Salisbury said, "though I only know, of course, what your master has told nic. I'm afraid, though, Ido not sympathise with these scoundrels so much as you do. justice is justice—an eye for an eye, a tooth fora tooth, a life for a "

He looked at John Brandon as he spoke, and laughed. "You agree with me, Jack, old chap, don't you?" he asked. "But, of course, you do. A little more tea, please. We don't get tea like this where I come from." .(To he continued.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE.
Cause Wrapped in Mystery.

Mr. Robert Dobson, coroner, held an inquest at the Stag Inn, Walton, on Tuesday, on the bodies of George Pickford (33),and Walter Reade (2(i), who were drowned in the Manchester Ship Canal, at Acton Grange the previous Friday. The facts as we recorded them last week were substantially correct. Since July a number of painters had been at work on the railway bridge which, at a height of 75 feet spans tbe canal, and to enable them to work on the underside a moveable cradle was constructed. This was a substantial apparatus weighing about 30 cwt., and con- structed largely of steel. What are technically termed "bangers " were attached to the girders of the bridge along which the cradle travelled these being so placed that the cradle suspender at each end always rested upon at least three. Every morning the painters on entering the cradle moved it in the required direction, it being returned to the end of the bridge when work ceased. On Friday the men arrived on the scene and, as is customary, an inspection was made of the cradle and the "hangers " and assured that everything was apparently in order and perfectly safe, five men entered the cradle and proceeded to propel it along the bridge, They had travelled about 30 feet when without any warning one end of the cradle became detached, and swung downwards, and three of the men were precipitated into the canal, two being drowned before assistance could be rendered. At the inquest Mr. Fenno, appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company. by whom the men were employed. Captain Wareing represented the Manchester Ship Canal Company whilst Superi- ntendent Ennion was present on behalf of the police. Mr. Fenna at the outset said that the directors and the officers of the Company were exceedingly sorry for the acCident. It was generally admitted that they had the very best appliances and that they had always kept them in good order and nothing gave them greater pain and sorrow than that the accident should have happened On behalf of the Company he desired to express deep sympathy with the relatives of the two men who were drowned. _ _ _

John Pickford, 14, Peel-street, Crewe, father of George Pickford, gave evidence of identification as did also John Reade, 7, Snow Hill, Nantwich. George Thomas Sewell, 3, Cowllelds, Nantwich, painters' labourer, spoke to the accident. Work had been in progress on the railway bridge at Acton Grange since July. On Friday morning operations commenced at half-past seven. "We had travelled from twenty to thirty feet from the side of the bridge "witness said "when I heard a cracking of wood and felt the cradle suddenly tip down at one end. land Albert Shakespear clung to the girder and shouted to some men who were on the top of the bridge, and told them to help the three men who had fallen into the canal. The men threw us some ropes and I fastened one round Shakespear and put the other round myself and we were drawn up." Witness added that he had not the least idea as to why the cradle gave way. The woodwork of part of the cradle was broken. When the cradle fell the suspender to which it was attached was left in position. In answer to Mr. Fenna, witness said that as far as he could see when they commenced work everything seemed in order and perfectly safe. The timber of the cradle was broken by the sudden drop of one end. He could not account for the accident at all. "Itis a perfect mystery." he said. Mr. Weir Vorild the wind have any effect on the cradle could not say. I should not say so. Mr. Weir: Was the cradle examined before work began ?—Yes, sir. The foreman inspected the cradle ibefore work began. Albert Shakespear, Nelson-street,Hightovvn,Plrexham,

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: said the cradle was examined before the men ventured upon it. He heard a crash and the next thing he knew he was pinned between one end of the cradle and the bridge. He did not know how the accident happened. John Boote, Nantwich, foreman in charge of the painters, said the "hangers " were all in position before the men went on to the cradle. He heard a crash and ran along the bridge. He beard someone shout "Your staging has given way "and ran off the bridge and down the embankment. When he got to the canal side a man named Davies had just been taken out of the water.

Mr. Dob§on : What caused the end of the cradle to give way ?"--I cannot say. It is a mystery to me. In answer to Mr. Fenna, witness stated that he was satisfied before the men went on to the cradle that everything was in perfect working order. The cradle worked steadily and properly. Mr. Prebble. A.M.1.C.E., divisional engineer in the employ of the L. and N.-W. Hailwly Company, stated that the cradle was constructed in 1893. It was thoroughly examined every time it went out of the shop and was last examined in June by a practical engineer. It was not possible for the cradle whilst being worked along the bridge to miss the " hangers" if they were in their proper position. He was on the scene shortly after the accident occurred and examined the whole of the appliances. Everything was in perfect order.
Mr. Fenna : Was there any flaw ?—Witness : There whs no flaw or strain of uny kind. Continaing he said he Ilan seen the cradle with nine men on it.
A Juror: It has broken. -cs:rt-h-Ke--on"it.—Witness nothing is broken. Mr. Dobson : What caused the end of the cradle to to become detatched ?—I cannot say.

Mr. Fenna : Mr. Prebble cannot tell and nor can any of the others. A Juror: Can anyone be produced who can tell us ' Mr. Fenna : We can find no one. We cannot manu- facture a cause. We state all we know and it is for the jury to decide. Upon the invitation of Mr. Fauna, the jury then pro- ceeded to inspect the bridge and a working model of the cradle. On their return after an absence of over an hour, Mr. Prebble, in answer to the coroner, said that Half the hangers and runners had been in position he could not explain the accident. A Juror : Were any of the hangers missing 2—N4ne whatever.

Mr. Weir: Do you think any displacement of the cradle could have been Paused by the wind ?—No. Inansvver to Mr. Fenna witness said he had never known a similar accident to happen before. He was satisfied that the apparatus could not in any way be improved. _ _ _

A Juror : If one end of the cradle had a big lead over the other would it miss the rollers ?—I am sure it would not. A Juror: If one runner missed a roller it would go into the water ?—lt\could not miss the roller. The Juror : You say not. Mr. Prebble : I have made all manner of experiments and find it cannot possibly miss. A Juror: Do you mean to allow it to remain as it is and allow men to work upon it ?—lt will be repaired and used again. I have every confidence in it. Mr. H. T. Purkiss, Lower Walton, said he saw the three men fall into the canal. He ran down to the edge of the water and succeeded in reaching a man named John Davies. The other two men were out of his reach. Captain Byfield, of the Runcorn Grappling Corps, spoke to the recovery of the bodies. After a short deliberation the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." They added that they found no fault with the construction of the cradle, but recom- mended that in future a boat and lifebelt should be pro- vided when similar work was being carried on.

div.head: MR. W. THORNE, M P, AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MR. W. THORNE, M P, AT WARRINGTON.
I

div.head: Value of Trade Unions.
div.p: The Value of Trade Unions.

On Tuesday evening, Mr. W. Thorne, M.P., one of the Labour representatives in the House of Commons, visited Warrington and addressed a meeting held under the auspices of the Warrington Branch of the Gasworker and general Labourers Union. The meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, Councillor Stott presiding over a large attendance. Mr. THORNE, who hid a healty reception said that it was evident all over the country that at the present time the hulk of the working classes were anxious to know more about the trade union and socialistic move- ment and he was convinced that when the present Parliament dissolved the Labour party would go back to the House of Commons very much stronger. "Applause). Having urged the value of trade utiions Mr. Thorne said he believed that eventually there would he a greater unity amongst the working classes. Trade unions were valuable organizations but individually they were not powerful enough to fight with success the power of organized capital which they now had to face. The defeat of one section Os the trade union forces was indirectly the defeat of every section of organized labour so that if they hoped to achieve their objects there must be one groat federation of trade unions. I (Hear, hear.) He had made up his mind that in the future he would preach an eight-hour day for all workers. Manufacturers would rather grant an increase of wages- than reduce the hours of labour for the simple reason that every reduction in the number of hours found employment for men on the street and brought about a reduction of the competition in the labour market. The average day worked by the 10,000,000 toilers in England was 10 hours. Reducing it to eight hours would find work for 2,000,000 people and would immediately solve the problem of unemployment, Mr. Thorne proceeded to refer to the question of com- pensation. What they desired to do was to adopt such a measure as would force employers to protect their machinery so that it would be almost impossible for the workees to be injured. In the Bill which would shortly pass the House of Commons and be submitted to the house of" mangleis " they had endeavoured to establish the principle that an injured workman should' receive compensation from the first day of the accident. (Applause.) They had not succeeded in their object but had established that if an accident incapacitated a man for nine days be should receive three days' pay but that if it extended over a fortnight he should get compensation from the day of the accident. (Applause.) Their principles in regard to the feeding of starving children werelmaking great headway in the country and the Government had now for the first time recognised the right that children should be fed by someone though theyhad made a mistake in deciding that local ratepayers should bear the cost. Next year education authorities would be empowered to raise a half pennY rate for the feeding of necessitous children. With regard to the children of drunken and idle parents it would bshould be taken from the parents they by the state but theY, ol altogether tboegtettehre r thatan d a must not rest until they had secured the adoption 01 the principle of the state maintenance of children. (Applause.) At the close Mr. Thorne was heartily 'thanked for his address.
