div.p: I
TOWN COUNCIL.
INCREASED PROFIT ON THE TRAMS.
Illness of Dr. Gornall.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday, when there were present :—The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Bolton), Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, W. J. Forshaw, J. Fairclough • Councillors T. Barton, W. Benson, T. Burton, T. Chantler, W. Clegg, J. G. Craik, E. Cunnington' J. Dickenson, D. S. Duncan, James Evans, L. Ellison, Dr. Joseph, J. Lord, J. J. Nield, J. Pergberton, J. Sankey, Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. F. Smith, F. Stott, 0. Poole, G. T. Wilding, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson, J. L. Whittle (town clerk), A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Deas (water engineer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), J. G. Gomall (medical officer), and J. M. Murray (director of education).

div.head: MAYOR'S THANKS.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S THANKS.

Before comMencing the business the MAYOR thanked the members of the Council and the officials, magis- trates, members of other public bodies and institutions, and the gentlemen of the town for their kindness in attending with him at St. Paul's Church on" Mayor's Sunday." He appreciated very warmly the support and assistance which have been so kindly tendered to him by all sections of the community since his ehction as Mayor, and hoped that with such support and assistance he would be able to carry out the duties in a way that would give satisfaction to all. (Applause.) The Mayoress and he had been the recipients of so very large a number of letters of congratulation that they had found it almost impossible to reply to all of them, and would be glad if ladies and gentlemen would accept their sincere thanks which he publicly tendered to them. (Applause.) THE LATE COUNCILLOR BROUGH. The MAYOR said: It is my paiaul duty to report to the Council the death of Mr. Councillor Brough. Mr. Brough entered the Council in 1901, and had been an extremely useful member. He served on many com- mittees, and in hi % patient labours he showed great discernment and stilknd judgment. Mr. Brough will be remembered by us, perhaps, more for the kindly way in which he treated all members of the Council. We have lost a very useful member, and one whom I think we all regarded as a personal friend. (Hear, hear.) I I beg to move:—" That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Mr. Walter Brough, a councillor of thigborough, which took place on the 22nd November, 1906, and requests the Town Clerk to convey to the widow and faintly of the late Mr. Brough this expression of the condolence of the Council with them in their bereavement." Councillor EVANS seconded and said be had known Mr. Brough for 30 years or more. He knew something of his work, and he felt from the standpoint of citizen- ship that Warrington was not the richer for his death. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe in using words of flattery on these occasions, but he would like to say' that he knew full well it was seldom, if ever, a claim I was made on the time, talents, or purse of Councillor Brough which was not responded to. He was sorry his place in the Council was vacant. Alderman BENNETT said the more he had know Mr. Brough the more highly he had thought of him. He was essentially an honest man, and he knew him to be a true Christian. But they thought of hi rc that night more in connection with his work as a member of the Corporation, and the admirable fidelity with which he discharged his duties, both on the Council and as a member of the Education Committee. All his work was typical of the high character which prompted his public and private actions. The whole town was the poorer for the loss of such a noble and truly honest character. (Hear, hear). Councillor PEmstatToN supported, and said he had been associated with the late Mr. Brough in connection with the Lawson Contract Committee, to which the deceased gave a great deal of time and intelligent work. If he had been spared to the Council he would have rendered still more valuable services to the ratepayers. They would all have been pleased if he had hem spared. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH observed that everything that had been said had been thoroughly deserved, anethere had been no exaggeration. Some people not knowing Mr. Brough might think all these things were exagger- ated, but those wh,-. had know the late Councillor intimately knew that what had been said was absolutely true.

Councillor BARTON thought a more pleasant, genial, or agreeable man he had never met or done business with. Councillor Borough had always a ray of sunshine upon his countenance, which rendered it pleasant to associate with him. He vras not happy unless he was trying to benefit someone, and the Council could ill afford to lose such a member. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BURTON corroborated what had been said, and said he had lost a close and valued friend. They would all feel his loss deeply.

The motion was carried: °- APPOINTMENTS. • Mr. W./ C. Brooks was appointed a member of the Board of Guardians on the Distress Committee in the place of the Rev. P. C. Mercer, resigned. Councillors Steel, Dickenson and Neild were appointed representative members of the Education Committee in the places of Councillor Brough, deceased, Mr. Thomas Wright, who has ceased to be a member of the Council, and Mr. Councillor Craik, resigned. The Mayor and Alderman Bennett were appointed representative governors on the governing body of the Warrington Grammar School.

div.head: ALDERMAN TINNION'S MOTION.
div.p: ALDERMAN TINNION'S MOTION.

First on the list of special motions came one by Alder- man Tinnion with reference to the minutes of the Council. The Alderman was not present at the meeting, and the MAYOR asked if any member of the Council i would make the motion n Alderman Tinnion's name. Councillor Loan rose to a point ororder, and urged that what the Mayor suggested could not be done. The MAYOR held that it was perfectly in order for any member of the Council to make the motion, but as no one offered to do so the next business was proceeded with.
BATHING ACCOMMODATION. COUNCIL AGREE TO CHEAPER BATHS.

Councillor STOTT moved :—" That in the opinion of this Conncil the time has arrived when steps should be taken to provide additional and cheaper bathing accommodation in Warrington." Two years ago they were promised that something should be done in that direction but the promise had not been carried out. He pointed out that there were few towns where the price for bathing was as high as in Warrington. They could not have a wash in a public bath in Warrington for less than 6d.' while a vapour bath cost Is. He knew many towns which only charged 3d. for a slipper bath and Gd. for a vapour bath, which placed them in the reach of workingmen. At Bradford, both swimming and slipper baths had been attached to a school, and they were open to the public in the even- ings at a charge of 2d. The Corporation ought to encourage those men who were engaged in dirty occupa- tions to wash their bodies and make them clean from a health standpoint. The objection was raised that they were losing money on the baths at the present time. If they looked at the question from a financial point of ' view, he did not think they would make much progress. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. He had always advocated that the working classes should have bathing facilities at a reasonable cost, but he would go so far as to say there should be free bathing. in the present baths there was a waste of space and the fittings were more elaborate than necessary. Private baths could be built at half the price of those they now possessed per bath, and would suit tha working classes. Councillor SKELLAND supported, and said the Council I ought to encourage cleanliness among men, women and children. Alderman BENNETT agreed with the resolution. It seemed to him that in a town like Warrington they ought at least to provide adequate facilities for the forming of habits of cleanli- ness. He would go further than many and I would make it absolutely obligatory upon builders to

put baths in the houses which they erected. He (Alder- man Bennett) strongly advocated the provision of baths in connection with the" Beamont School, but, unfor- tuttately, he was unable to get his wishes adopted. In the light of the new experience, however, the Education Committee, backed by the Council, should see their way to provide at every school which served a big area,whore there was no bathing accommod&tion at present, facili- ties which might be utilized for the benefit of the residents in the neighbourhood. It appeared to him that the Conncil had a genius for forgetting what they had previously decided. The Council passed a resolu- tion 12 or 15 years ago in favour of the provision of open- air baths, and why that had not been oarried out be failed to see. It was comparatively easy to 'provide open-air baths, and he suggested that Victoria Park should be thrown open, and that a bath should be pro- vided there.

Councillor ELLISON also sppported the resolution. Alderman BOLTON said the matter did not rest with the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee. If the Council would find the money the Committee would carry schemes out. They had already paid £11,433 for their baths, and there was a loss on them of £471 a year. If the Council would give the committee about £lO,OOO the committee would give them all the baths they wanted. He thought the best thing they could do would be to let the Baths Committee or one of the officials report to the Council or committee upon the way the cheaper baths could be obtained, so that the ratepayers should not be overburdened with another Technical School at a fanoy expense. Councillor LORD said the town had so much water that they did not know what to do with it. Why pay a bath tax? If the tax was taken away it might induce builders to put baths in cottage wroperty. The resolution was unanimously approved.
PUBLICATION OF COUNCIL MINUTES. PRESS TO BE AGAIN SUPPLIED.

Councillor LORD moved :—" That Standing Order 10 be rescinded, and 'that all minutes of committees (except those considered by the respective committees of a private nature) shall be printed upon the Council agenda, and copies shall be sent to members of the Council, Press, Property Owners' Association, Trades- men's Association, Trades and Labour Council, and any other public body. rill minutes left off the Council agenda by order of any committee shall be printed on a separate and supplementary agenda, this supplemental agenda to also contain a list of all tenders, and prices, and to be supplied to members of the Council only." He said that under the old Standing Order it had been possible so keep minutes of importance as well as minutes not of importance off the Council agenda, with the result that the Council had been placed in the awkward position,of passing schemes of which they had known nothing, notably, schemes relating to the pur- chase of property. If the motion in Alderman Tinnion's name had been passed the Council would have been in such a position that they would have had to wade through eighteen minute books to see if there was any, thing in the minutes of any committee that had not appeared in the agenda. Councillor WELDING seconded.

Conncillor PEMBERTON said the Council had expresed itself on two or three occasions and had said that they would not have secrecy in regard to to any matters. He, Councillor Lord, and other members of the Council, agretd that it would not be wise te make matters public while-they were in an unsettled state, but it was only right that every Councillor should know what was going on in order that the Corporation's business might be properly transacted. There had been too much secrecy in the past. DrAOSEcif said he believed in the Press having copies of the agenda, but, he asked, why such bodies as the Property Owners' Association, Tradesmen's Association, Trades and Labour Council, &c., should have them ? Where was it going to end ? Councillor PEMBERToN : It has been the custom.

The DEPUTY MAYOR said all this Would be very nice if it was feasible, but he did not see how they would keep private matters from leaking out into quarters where they might result in detriment to the'Conncil. To reply to Council.CLEGO,

The 'AIAYOR said it had 'been the custom to also supply the Library with copies of the agendas. Councillor BuirroN : I take it that Councillor Lord does not intend that the supplemental agenda should be handed round. He had been in the Council ten years and he did not know yet what was going on in connec- tion with the waterworks. It was only the Investiga- tion Committee who knew ; the remainder of the Coun- cil were dummies. They were told that it was such a serious matter that it was not fit for them to know. (Laughter): He was getting tired of it all. Councillor WILKINsoN : I take exception to ` secrecy." There are only a few people in the Council who are in the habit of snivelling and smiling and talking about secrecy. I The MAYou : Now you should not use those words !

, Councillor WIKINSON : It's nothing, The MAYOR : You were talking about snivelling. (La ugh ter.) Councillor WILKINSON : That's all right ; you will find it in the dictionary. (Laughter.) The reason that Standing,Order No, 10 was repealed was that they con- sidered it inadvisiable for matters to get to the public before they were in a matured state, They would be fools and asses if they divulged matters before they were matured. What would they think of the business man who divulged his intentions before he completed a transaction ? He saw in the papers that someone connected with one paper rather prided himself that he had run against one of the agendas in the street. Alderman BOLTON : One of the Council supplied it.

Councillor WILKINSON The wind blew it against him. (Laughter.) I rather smile at them talking about secrecy when they find agendas floating in the air. The ratepayers must understand that nothing was kept from them. The men who said there was secrecy were telling lies.

Councillor PEMBERTON : I object to that remark. Councillor ‘VILKINSON : Why should you take it upon your shoulders? Councillor PEMBERTON : I am one who said there was secrecy, and it applies to me. Councillor WILKINSON : I am not alluding to you at all. We have had too much secrecy. Councillor PEMBERTON: Hear, hear. (Laughter.) Councillor WILKINSON said if certain of them wanted to know what was going on they should get on to the committees.

A VOICE : They cannot. Councillor STOTT supported the resolution, although, he said, it did not altogether meet with his views, fie wanted it to be made impossible for members of the Council to say that things were being done secretly. Councillor LOAD said Councillor Wilkinson's memory was evidently very short. They had had too much secrecy, as a result of which the Council had previ- ously been placed in a very ignominious position. The resolution was carried.

div.head: STREET LIGHTING.
div.p: STREET LIGHTING.

Councillor STEEL drew the attention of the Lighting Sub-committee to the irregular lighting of the lamps in Battersby-lane and Marsh House-lane. The lamps, he sai/Ititwere Aot lighted early enough, and were ex- tinguished too early. Councillor ELLisoN wished to remind the sub-com- mittee of their promise to fix lamps in Poachers-lane. (Laughter.) Councillor LORD supposed every member, on behalf of his particular ward, would desire to call attention to its lighting. (Laughter.) Councillor Toorm : I wish to call the attention of the Council to the lighting in Bewsey-ward. (Loud laughter,) _ . _

Connelllor EVANS said the committee had already paid attention to the lighting of the Marsh House-lane district. That district happened to be one where the lamplighters met, and if they were to reverse the order of things, some other district would be similarly affected. They had not yet arrived at that state of perfection whereby all the lamps in the town could be lighted at once. He would, however, mention the matter to the Gas Engineer.
The minutes were passed. DR. GORNALL'S HEALTH..
TEMPORARY ASSISTANCE TO BE ENGAGED.

Councillor EVANS in moving the adoption of the Health Committee's minutes, desired to call attention to a matter of some urgency which did not appear on the minutes. Dr. Gornall had not been well for some time and it was necessary that he should take a fairly long rest. The committee found that they would have to procure for him some assistance to cope with his ever- increasing duties. During the last few week a local medical practitioner had been assisting him. The com- mittee found that the increase of work had been principally occasioned by, the administration of the Education Act and new methods. The Medical Officer was responsible for the medical examination of school children. Last year Dr. Gornall examined over 1,000 school children and found over 500 with defective eye- sight. Whilst in other towns that work was done by a medical gentleman employed only by the Education Committee, the Health Committee were anxious that . . _

the supervision of the medical examination of scholars should rest with the borough Medical Officer. The committee had, therefore, invited applications for an assistant medical officer, to be employed temporarily, and they were in favour of engaging a lady physician and surgeon, whose salary would be £125. This matter however, had still to come before the Council.

Councillor -EIT-RT-ON—s—eConded the adoption of the 1 minutes. He believed that Dr. Gornall's ill-health had been brought about by over-work. He had not had a ' holiday for two years. Councillor Dr. JosErn said there was only one objec- tion to a lady doctor, and that was whether she would be able to maintain dicipline over the other ladies in the Council's employ. He thought, however, that this lady had all the tact and the administrative qualities necessary to steer clear of any difficulties. She was qualified as a physician and surgeon and had generally high educational attainments. Councillor S rorr said that although this appointment was only a temporary one, he believed they would have to obtain permanent assistance. More systematic atten- tion would have to be given to the school children, and he thought they ought to have a medical officer speci- ally for that department. Councillor WILKINSON thought the Health Committee were taking the wrong track. A man should be obtained for the education department alone. Alderman EVANS : Councillor Evans is only prepar-

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: ing the Council for a future resolution. When the com- mittee have decided the matter it will come up for con- firmation. _ .

Councillor PEMSEArC)SI observed that when the resolu- tion came the Council would find that the committee had gone so far with the appointment that they could not oppose their action. Permanent assistance was evidently required, and it was a pity that the cotnmittee had gone so far. The minutes were passed. GREENGATE BRICKS. A MISTAKE EXPLAINED.

lln moving the adoption of the Sauitary Works Com- mittee's minutes,Alderman EVA NS said that unfortunately an advertisement appeared asking for tenders for Green- , gate bricks. It was a mistake on the part of the I manager and directly he (Alderman Evans) saw it, he communicated with him ancyadvised him to withdraw the advertisement. That was done and the advertise- ment would appear afresh in Saturday's papers. The MAYOR : It appeared last Saturdak. Councillor PEMBERTON thought it was a pity that any particular make of brick was mentioned in the adver- tisement. It ought to be sufficient to specify" St. Helens bricks." Aldermon EVAN'S : I think I have explained that. It was not the intention of the Committee to have Green- ' cate bricks. It was an unfortunate mistake made by the manager. The advertisement has been withdrawn land he was instructed to advertise for wire-cut bricks. or equal thereto. Councillor PEMBERTON said he objected to the hdvertisentent which stated " Greengate or equal : thereto." His contention was that it would be sufficient to say St. Helens brick, or equal thereto." The brick was made out of a common clay and there were quite half a dozen makers of similar bricks. He defied anyone when they were building a wall to tell the difference. Sometimes when the bricks were out of the wall, it was impossible to say which works they came from. He did not think any special make,but only the particular district,sEould be set up as a sample. That was the CASO with ltuabon bricks which included many different makes. The minutes were approved. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

It being his 60th birthday, the Paving and Sewerage Committee passed a vote of congratulation to` the Borough Surveyor. Councillor CuAix moved the confirmation 6f the minutes, and asked the permission of the Council for the committee to finish the work of paving in Bridge- street before the snow and frost came. It would be far better for the work to be proceeded with. Councillor IVILKINsoN seconded. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH drew attention to the condi- tion of the wood pavement in Museum-street. There were, he said, almost more holes than paving. (Laughter). It was not safe to walk along it, and it was surprising horses' legs had not been broken. Councillor STOTT, referring to a resolution of the committee, that Councill9r Craik be appointed the deputy-chairman, said that gentleman would make an admirable vice-chairman, but he thought considering his long experience and lengthy services to the com- mittee, Councillor Pemberton ought to have been selec- ted.
The MAYOR,: The matter rests with the committee and not with the Council. The minutes were agreed to. SUNDAY OPENING AT THE MUSEUM.

It was resolv ed that the question of Sunday opening be put upon the agenda for the next meeting of the Museum Committee. The minutes were agreed to without comment on the motion of Alderman BENNETT, seconded by Councillor ELLisoN. UNEMPLOYED PAINTERS.

At a meeting of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Com- mittee, a letter was read from Councillor Stott asking the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee to arrange for the work of painting the baths to be carried out as early as possible in order to find work for unemployed painters. The Town Clerk was instructed to reply that as nothing was provided in the present estimates, the committee did not propose to carryout the work during the ensuing winter. LIGHTING OF STOCKTON HEATH.

At a recent meeting of the Gas Committee a letter was read from the Clerk to' the Rural District Council of Runcorn, complaining of the unsatisfactory manner in which the street lamps were lighted at Stockton Heath. The Gas Committee passed a resolution to the effect that they were of the opinion thht there was no real ground for complaint, but in order to give the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee an opportunity of carrying oat the lighting more effectively if they could, the committee would be prepared to supply gas in bulk at the usual price, and hand over the lighting and care ot the lamps to that committee on terms to be arranged. On the motion of Councillor DUNCAN, seconded by the DEPUTY-MAYOR, the minutes were agreed to.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF MR. KINSLEY.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF MR. KINSLEY.

It was reported to the Gymnasium ,Committee that Mr. J. E. L. Kinsley had tendered his resignation as gymnasium instructor. It was resolved that the com- mittee place on record their great regret on losing his services, and their high appreciation of the very valu- able services rendered by him fora period of 14 yams.

div.head: PHYSICAL INSTRUCTION.
div.p: PHYSICAL INSTRUCTION.

- The CHAIRMAN reported the result of the interview which the special committee appointed at the last meet- ing had had with the School Management Committee, and submitted the following amended resolution of the latter committee :—" That the Gymnasium Committee he approached with a view to ascertaining upon what terms they would be prepared (a) to provide a class at the Gymnasium for the instruction of teachers who have not got a certificate or qualification for the teaching of physical exercises ; and (b) to arrange for the instruc- ' t ion of the pupil teachers and Secondary School scholars in physical exercises at the Gymnasium by the instruc- tors of the Gymnasium during the year commencing on the Ist of November' 1903." It was resolved that the School Management Committee be informed that the committee would be prepared to provide facilities for the classes they required for £5O per annum. Alderman EvaNs moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor CLEGG seconded, and the motion was agreed to. REPAIRS OF THE TRAMWAY TRACE. At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee the Town Clerk reported that at the last meeting of the Council the resolutions as to the repair of the tramway track were defeated, and it was resolved that the Chairman and Deputy-Chairman be appointed to meet the Chairman and Deputy-Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee with a view to devising a scheme for the carrying out of the repairs, and that pending a settlement of the question, temporary arrange- ments be made with Mr. James Briscoe for the carrying out of the work in accordance with specification and schedule of prices. EARLY CARS. A petition from residents in the neighbourhood of the Cemetery was read asking the committee to run early morning cars on that route, and it was resolved, that the request be granted. The IVIAvom moved the confirmation of the mimutes. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded. _ _ . _

Councillor STEEL said a number of workmen had complained to him that the early cars on the route named were not suitable. One of the cars left at 5%30 and the other at 5.50. The workmen were somewhat of a superior class and did not go to work before 7 or 7.30. It was suggested that the cars should run between 6.30 and 6.45.
The MA.YOR said the matter had already been taken into consideration and the time altered. PROFIT ON THE ELECTRICITY AND TRAMWAYS UNDERTAKINGS. _

The MAYoFt. submitted the following statement :—t. have pleasure in announcing that the electricity depart- ment has not only been able to hold its own during the summer months. but that the working has resulted in a net profit Of £172. This is a reduction in comparison with last year of £ll9, but it is very satisfactory when it is taken into consideration that the price of current has been reduced to the tramways department and also to consumers for power purposes. (Hear, hear.)—l have also pleasure in announcing that for the half-year ended 30th September, 1906, the gross profit on the tram- ways undertaking amounted to £4,109 19s. 6d., as against £3,3T8 4s. 10d. for the corresponding period last year. being an increase of ,C 731 14s. Bd. The sinking fund and interest charges have been met out of this, leaving a net profit of £1,193 18s. 7d. as against .C.. 489 6s. 3d., an increase of £733 12s. 4d. This extra profit is accounted for by increased passenger receipts amounting to .V 177 4s. Id. The large increase in the traffic receipts of the Stockton Heath route is chiefly owing to the extension having been working for a half-year, whereas in 1902 only two months' reeeipts were included. An increased income of £2O has also been received for advertising on cars. The working expenses have been reduced £36. The traffic expenses have gone op £l2O owing to the running of an extra car on the Stockton Heath route for six months against three months last year, but this increase has been more than counter- balanced by a saving in the general expenses and maintenance charges. The result can, therefore, be regarded as satisfactory, bat it ought to be borne in mind that the summer is the best half-year for traffic receipts, and also that the price of electric current has been redtfced this year. (Applause.)
Councillor WILKINSON seconded the confirmation of the minutes.

Councillor STOTT said the Mayor's statement seemed Ito indicate that the more they reduced tram fares, the 'greater the profit. That should encourage the com- mittee to go In for half-penny stages. Alderman BENNETT congratulated the Mayor on the highly satisfactory result which was a very pleasing beginning to his worship's Mayoralty. The statement showed that municipal management paid, if it was , proper management. He saw from a recently published list that Warrington made more profit from municipal undertakings than any other municipality, with one exception. The minutes were passed.

div.p: THE LAWSON CONTRACT.

div.head: PROP WY PURCHASES.
div.p: PROP WY PURCHASES.
£40,000 TO BE BORROWED.
Councillor Pemberton's Challenge to the Council.

At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening, it was reported that the General Purposes Committee considered the list of properties purchased for street improvements, and after discussion it was resolved, that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £40,139 13s. ad., being the cost incurred in acquiring properties for street widenings. It was further resolved that the property purchased from Mrs. Jane Fairhurst, in Buttermarket-street, be not included in the above application. The MAYOR formally moved the confirmation of the minutes.

Councillor Cr.mou alluded to the property purchased from Mrs. Jane Fairhurst and contended that the Council had been entirely misled with reference to this matter. He (Councillor Clegg) had been supplied with a list of properties purchased and it included the item to which he now called attention. The property was described as a warehouse (empty) in Buttermarket- street, and under the column " rents if any " appeared £47. The natural conclusion to be drawn from that was that if the warehouse were occupied it would produce £47 for the rates of the borough. The purchase price was £2,200. In times past the officials of the Corporation had been charged with making things appear very rosy, but in this case the facts were not correct. The property covered over 300 square yards of land, and included, in addition to the warehouse, a house and shop. It had a frontage to Buttermarket-street of from 12 to 14 yards and that,was one of the narrowest and most dangerous parts of Buttermarket-street. He moved that this item be referred back.

author of interesting and powerful stories which have appeared in several newspapers under the nom-de-plarac of Lumley Harbet. There were large congrega- tions at Sunday's services and Mr. Harbottle delivered excelleut discourses. In the morning his subject was "The deliverance of Peter from prison." He pointed out that the chapter in which this event was described —Acts xiit—was one of the most dramatic in the Bible. It Vas like a drama in five acts. One scene was laid in Herod's palace, which represented material power ; the second showed Peter in prison, represent- ing human weakness. Then the scene moved to the house of Mary where the many were gathered together praying—representing belief in spiritual power—and it ended tragically when Herod was smitten. The great question in the affairs of our own life and in things touching the Church, said the preacher, was to know what was going on in heaven. If we only knew what they were thinking and determining upon in heaven, we would never allow ourselves to be distressed at all. The Church was driven to prayer by the imprisonment of Peter—which might, to many people, seem a weak thing to do, but it had its answer. If the Church to-day, could only recover the ancient belief in prayer,all things would be possible to her. When the Church came together for prayer, something was sure to happen. In these days when the Church came together it was often to read papers, and if they called the church together for prayer, few people responded. He would that it were otherwise, for it was by prayer that great things could be accomplished. The choir effectively rendered the Te Deuneto Jack- son's setting. In the afternoon a successful musical service was held, Alderman Tinnion presiding. The choir gave a very creditable interpretation of the anthem" Send out Thy Light." Mrs. Arthur Booth sang with much feeling "0 Divide Redeemer " (Gounod) and " Hear ye Israel " (Mendelssohn) and Miss Armstrong was heard to advantage in 0 Rest in the Lord." Cornet solos entitled " The lost chord " and "The star of Bethlehem" by Mr.W. Rutter were a pleasing feature At the evening service the Rev. G. Harbottle preached on "The three crosses of Calvary." He said there were three great words which guided one to the meaning of thedeath of Christ—love,substitution, and propitiation. The Cross represented for man the great opportunity and the great promise. The choir again acquitted themselves admirably in "And the glory of the Lord" from "The Messiah.' At the close of the service Mr. T. W. Pearce gave a most enjoyable organ recital, his selections including " The Storm" (Lemmens), "Festive March " (Smart) and " Aadante in G" (E. Batiste). The collections for the day amounted to about £1 2. "GRAVE AND GAY." LECTURE FtY REV. G. HARBOTTLE. On Monday evening the Rev. G. Harbottle delivered a highly interesting lecture entitled "Grave and Gay." There was a fair attendance, Mr. John Taylor, L.D.S., presiding. The (211/ORMAN referred to his thirty-one years association with Bewsey-road Church and recalled the fact that be listened to the first sermon preached in the building. He dwelt upon the many changes which had taken place during that period and also alluded to Mr. Harbottle's happy ministry in the Warrington circuit. The Rev. G. HARBOTT LE pointed out that 'there was a grave and a gay side to everything. These two aspects in nature were expressed in nature's own way in the alternation of night and day. The lecturer vividly pictured the awe-inspiring silence of night in such a wild district as the Derbyshire Downs and contrasted it with the brightness of daybreak. Continuing he said it seemed to him that the best life was that in which the grave and th 3 gay were mingled in fair prop )rtions. They must not cultivate gravity to the entire exclusion of gaiety, or rice versa. The man who had deep seriousness in him but who could let humour play like summkir lightning over the surface of his life was the man who was most to his (the speaker's) heart. Mr. Harbottle then dealt entertainingly with gravity and gaiety as exemplified in babies. The best managed of all our institutions, he continued, was the home, and the honour and glory for that mast go to woman. If one could only feel sure that woman could manage the government of the countryios well, one would be con- tent to see one's grandmother on the Woolsack, one's mother as Prime Niinis'er, rind one's sister—or the other fellow's sister w 11.) \vas atv.iy., more interesting—hold- ing various otflc"s in the Govarement. (Laughter.) The Lecturer nest dealt with oir buys." To have been a boy, he said. was to have touched the highest point of human felicity, and to have survived perils compared with which the adventures of soldiers, sailors, and hunters for big game were mere trifles. (Laughter.) The great problem of the Church to-day was how to retain " our boys" who were drifting from it. In almost every congregation, one was struck with the absence of young men. The Puritanical con- ception of religion was too stern for boyhood, and it was equally certain that the cavalier repre- sentation of religious life did not produce the kind of men who were wanted. They must have mingled gravity and gaiety in their religion if they were to retain their young men. The minister who appealed to " our boys "mast first of all be a man and secondly a minister. Mr. Harbottle touched upon the gravity and tghaa i et ttyh oouf gl ho vdeeatahndw a pd or el igtai ds eadn,rvi tehnsdei cdh bgyr epaot isnotlieumg nOittlyt there were not wanting men who had managed to intro- duce an'element of gaiety in the most terrible circum- stances into the solemn matter of cl.ring. He quoted examples from .history, including that of Charles IT. who apologised for having been such an unconscion- able long time in dying." The lecturer exhorted his hearers so to live that their last hour, while being toll of solemnity would also be illumined with brightness and joy. A vote of thanks to the lecturer concluded the meeting.

THE TRADES Lords was engaged in DISPUTES BILL. summing up its own char- acter. It was an astounding and melancholy business. How any such section of the people as is entitled to be respected for the weight of its opinion can in future regard the House of Lords as a body with a right to claim the shaping of legislation, we are quite unable to understand. The business dealt with on Tuesday was the Trades Disputes Bill. That measure, as the LORD CHANCELLOR reminded the House, left the House of Commons with a unani- mous endorsement. Lord LORERURN was deliver- ing a conciliatory speech, and for this reason he said nothing of the events which led up to this unanimity. He did not tell their lordships, for instance, that Mr. BALFOIJR had fought the Bill throughout all its stages with an opposition that seemed to be almost vicious, and had then, at the last moment, been converted to new views with as much suddenness as if the change in his opinion had been the result of a vision of the night. Of course, all persons with any power of political discernment under- stood the reason for Mr. BALFOUR'S sudden collapse and transformation. It came about not because he loved the Trades Disputes Bill more, but because he did not like to contemplate the effect of a rejection or rnultilation of that Bill if it should be followed by another General Elec- ion. Lord LANSDOWNE, pursuing Mr. BALFOUR'S lines, stated the case with simple and amazing frankness in the House of Lords.

After certain more or less judicious preliminaries, Lord LANSDOWNE advised their lordships to accept the Bill, as, in fact, they did, on the understanding that there was to be an attempt to save their faces in Committee. Now, what were his reasons? They have the utmost importance in their bearing upon the Education Bill. Lord LA.NSDOWNE said, first of all, that the trend of legislation had for many years past been strongly in favour of a fuller recognition of the rights of trade unions. The decision of the House of Lords in its judicial capacity in Igol had been a great surprise. At least, it had been a great surprise to most people. The question had come before the constituencies. The Labour vote had all gone one way. He did not much believe in the cant about mandates, but if there ever was a mandate it was the decision of the electors at the last General Election in favour of restoring the old status of trade unions. In this smooth—we might almost be justified in saying sleek—tone, Lard LANSDOWNE went on endeavour- ing to mitigate the sullen feelings of the peers sitting behind him. Legislation of this kind, he said, was inevitable. It would have been equally inevitable if he and his friends had been sitting on the Government Benches. Then he went on to explain what he believes to be the function of the House of Lords. It is to arrest the progress of such measures its have not been sufficiently con- sidered and to destroy those which, in the opinion of the House of Lords, are not in harmony with the wishes of the people. This was all in the nature of what Pope calls "leather and prunella." The important paint was that whilst considering this Bill a bad Bill, Lord LA,NsnowNE advised the House of Lords to accept it. His reasons, we have no hesitation in saying, were base and cop- temptible. He believes that the Bill contains the possibilities of all manner of mischief, yet he will permit it to pass. Why ? Because he wishes to secure the acqaiescence ot the Labour party in the Lords' treatment of the Education Bill. There was a very fierce speech from that every able old man, the ER-LORD OFIANCELLOR, who said that he had never acquiesced in any proposed course with greater reluctance. The Bill was unjust, it was opposed to the spirit of English liberty, it con- tained a section more disgraceful than any that had ever appeared on any English statute. It was a Bill for the purpose of legalising tyranny. It would produce commercial distress, industrial war- fare, and something verging on civil war. Its con- sequences would be evil, and it was in itself a serious blow to public freedom. We will suppose Lord HALSBURY to believe all this. What, then, are we next to believe ? He and the party to which he belongs take all the risks. They will dare evil and suffering. They will dare civil war; they will dare anything in order to compel the children of Dissenters to

'accept the teaching of the Established Church. They accept the Trades Disputes Bill in order that they may have a free hand with the Education Bill. That, in colloquial language, is " the long and the short of it."

In future we shall not THE COUNCIL require to lay an ambush MINUTES. for the capture of one of the Council agendas con- taining the minutes of committees. Standing Order No. JO which debarred the issue of the agendas to the Press was rescinded on Tuesday after a brief but lively career. As substitutes for it there were two resolutions, one in the name of Alderman Tinnion and the other proposed by Councillor Lord. As the Alderman was away in London his motion fell to the ground and the Council adopted Councillor Lord's proposals with out a dissentient vote. We said last week that we preferred this particular resolution, and now that it is in force there should be no question of secrecy in the future so far as committee business is concerned. All minutes (except those con. sidered by the respective committees to be of' a private nature) will be printed on the agenda, copies of which are to be supplied to the Press and all public bodies in addition to the members of the Council. The advocates of publicity have thus gained an important point, and one which it was essential to insist upon if public confidence in municipal management was ever to be secured. It is worth while noting, to), that the resolution provides that the confidential minutes shall be printed upon a supplemental agenda which will be supplied to members of the Council only. There is something gained here, for previously any business which any Committee chose to keep secret was kept from the Councillors as a whole. Now, the unquestion- able right of every member of the Council to know all about everything which comes within the purview of committees is recognised. This should do away with the possibilities of such an anomaly recurring as that mentioned by Councillor Burton, who said he had been in the Council ten years and did not know yet what was being done in con- nection with the waterworks. There have been too many committees which have in the past carried on their business like rival firms. Co-operation and not rivalry is what the town requires between the different departments of the Corporation, and the new standing order should help to bring about a better state of things.
The Town Council unani- BATHING mously passed a motion by AccommonATloN. Councillor Stott on Tues-

day to the effect that " the time has arrived when steps, should be taken to provide additional and cheaper bathing accom- modation in Warrington." Of course, the' resolution does not commit the Council to anything beyond an expression of opinion, or else there would probably not have been such charming unanimity on the question. Coun- cillor Stott will have to keep pegging away if he wants anything done, for resolutions of this kind have a way of being considered oncP, and then getting shelved for a few years. The Baths Com • mittee must be kept on the qui vive and pressed for a scheme which will increase the very inadequate bathing (in the double meaning of the word) accommodation in Warrington. Our present public baths are I very efficient, but they do not supply the wants of the masses, and developments on the lines of open-air swimming baths, and workmen's slipper baths are essential in a town like Warrington, which now lays claim to being well-governed. There has been a large reduction of municipal expenditure in recent years, and with the rates now at a more satisfactory figure, improvement schemes on legitimate lines may fairly be put upon the table. The town cannot stand still. It must either go forward or backward, and having rested on its oars for a reasonable period, the natural , course is obviously forward towards the goal of the greatest good for the greatest number.

With next Monday even- THE JUNIOR ing's meeting the Junior LIBERALS. Liberal Association brings to a close the first part of the winter session. The members have every reason to feel encouraged by the work already accomplished—in fact they may be pardoned for indulging feelings of pride that such a young organization has already proved itself a powerful force on the Progressive side. The syllabus drawn up for this session was an ambitious one and the interest taken in the varied subjects introduced augurs well for the educational influ- ence of the Association. There have been some admirable papers on topics of moment, and it is a noteworthy fact that, although the assistance of' outsiders has been c3rdially welcomed, the members have also acquitted themselves with credit in this direction. The tone of the meetings has been distinctly high, and it has beenH fully evident that the " juniors " have given not a little thought to the questions brought forward. Another groat advantage of the Association is that it serves to cultivate debating powers i and it has also discovered budding orators who are sure to be heard supporting the Progressive cause in the future. We would call special attention to the fact that a large attendance is hoped for at next Monday's meeting as the subject for discussion—" The taxation of land values "—is one of great import upon which all Liberals :should seek to be thoroughly well informed. A delegate from the English League which is propagating this much-needed reform will deliver:an address. The hearing of the West THE WEST RIDING Riding Appeal in the House APPEAL. of Lords is a reminder of

the singularity of these proceedings in the highest judicial tribunal of the land. Immediately beneath the Press Gallery, at the end of the building, has been visible the Attorney-General's wig. That legal luminary stands immediately before the Lord Chancelldr (with his back to the Press) in a plain wooden box, which in an ordinary court of assize a visitor would have no difficulty in identifying as the dock. The Solicitor-General and Mr. S. A. T. Rowlatt have occupied the seats of the warders. In the assize court, too, as those will remember whom either misfortune or curiosity ha l taken thither, his Lordship's place is on the dais—high and lifted up—under the shadow of an impos- ing , canopy surmounted by fantastically-carved figures of a rampant lion and unicorn. In the House of Lords the Lord Chancellor sits in the lowest place, at a cross-table on the floor of the building, in such state as would seem proper to a clerk in a polling-booth if he did not raise his wig, from time to time, to scratch his head. Half-a-dozen Law Lords (who are not provided with wigs) saunter in as though they had just come down to breakfast, and, gathering up their coat-tails, take their seats on the front benches. For the rest the House is a wilder. ness of red leather with red buttons in it. At long intervals one or two visitors emerge from behind a curtain at the other end of the building, but their footfalls are noiseless on the dark-green carpet, and the proceedings go forward in the low voices of intellectual and aristocratic detachment which so picturesquely represent total oblivion of the existence of the general public. Indeed, the stranger probably retires behind the curtain with the conviction that the supreme qualification for a place in the Press Gallery is an abnormal development in the organ of hearing. He may even wonder why the Press are not given a different position.

A cabman, making for Victoria Station, drove for some distance alongside a funeral without trying to cross it. But at last he said to the hearse-driver in a cabman's whisper : " Look 'ere ! my 'fare's in a 'urry and yours ain't." :u The man who twistda Cow's tail off at a farm near Crewe deserved more than the penalty of ~-e3 and costs which the magistrates imposed. If Ile had been sent to goal for 3 months it would have been a punish- ment more fitting such an inhuman and cruel act. Some men need teaching a lesson occasionally and this was one of those instances where justice should not have been tempered with mercy. o

'There were explosions galore at Messrs. Crosfield's works on Wednesday evening. lembers of the fire brigade were actually on the scene, but they did not manifest alarm or even excitement. Moreover the explosions were deliberately premeditated. They formed part of the experiments to illustrate o highly interesting lecture on "A history of discovery in flame."

* * Sankey-street was, not long ago, the worst-paved main street in the town. Its mantle seems to have descended upon Museum-street, which according to Dr: Joseph, contains more holes than paving. The surface of this street is certainly in a terrible state, but it will probably have to wait its turn. Fortun- ately the amount of traffic in that neighbourhood is not grea\. * * * The maily friends of the Rev. George Harbottle, who at one time worked in the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit, are always pleaded to welcome him to the old town. He is an attractive and powerful speaker and his sermons and lecture at Bewsey-road Church last week-end were listened to with much interest by large assembles. Originality,is one of Kr. Harbottle's strong points and in his entertaining lecture he was able to picture a grave and a gay side to most things. His advice was admirable : Let the grave and the gay be mingled in fair proportions in the affairs of life, not ' allowing either to entirely dominate them. * * The St. Helens police are elaborate and even theatrical in their methods of securing convictions against the betting fraternity. In a case this week in which John Banks was fined £lO for using the Hawk and Buck Inn for betting,a young police officer related the novel methods by which he trapped the offender. The " P.C." worked as a labourer for 6 weeks in the neighbourhood and made himself a favourite at the Hauk and Buck. " I danced for them, I sang for them, I played billiards with the landlord, and I got !to know all the customers," he said in his evidence. After this, who can charge our' men in blue,with want of fertility and resource ? Our St. Helens friend must be a budding Lecoeq. * * *

We are sorry to see such a paper as the " Gentle- woman " expressing such a depraved idea of Sunday as the following : "Sunday is not a popular day in England. To the average person it seems to be a day of complete boredom, and even those who bridge and golf, and motor and cycle, seem to find Sunday more irksome than any other day of the seven." It seems to us that this is a libel on the " average person." Apparently the " Gentlewoman " has for- gotten that the general custom in the country is to observe the Sabbath on Christian lines. There may well be tendencies towards the secular Sunday when people persist in considering it a day of boredom I instead of counting it a day of rest. 0 A house to house collection is to take place next , week in Warrington and district on behalf of the clearly 2,000 Lancashire children freely admitted to r Dr. Barnado's Homes during the past few years, of which number 10 have been from Warrington. Last year £5 Bs. was raised here, and it is honed to exceed that sum next week. In the thirty-nine years ,of his work among homeless waifs the late Dr. Barnardo rescued over 59,000 boys and girls. At the time of his death, about 8,000 orphans or otherwise destitute children—many of them blind, deaf, dumb, crippled or feeble-minded—were being cared for in the Homes bearing his name. The great work of saving the children is being Continue! by the Council who assisted him during his life. , . •• .

The Rev. H. Minnie() has not lost the knack of speaking plainly and at a social re-union between himself and mans' oid Warrington friends on Monday night he had some interesting things to say. For instance' Warrington was "a clannish town, the most clannish he ever knew," but he would have stayed in Warrington if he had had a trust deed broad enough to have enabled him to build up the kind of church he wanted. Mr. Minnie() had to undergo some " chaff " about his friend and colleague, the I.),ev. C. F. Aked, being "called "to New York. He replied that if ever he left the Christian Ministry "it would be to enter Parliament as a Socialist." Mr. Dunnico's work is prospering in Liverpool, and in addition to the con- gregation at Kensington Church having doubled, he has a gathering of 400 or 500 men every Sunday afternoon.

* * * Most people attribute the reluctance with which they rise from bed of a winter's morning to a certain weakness in their own moral fibre, but the " Lancet " this week unburdens our consciences by enunciating the comfortable doctrine that the sluggishness is not moral but physical. It is the sun's fault ;he is not only a late riser himself in winter, but the cause of late rising in others. The sun's rays are full of activities, and they exert a stimulus upon both the 'mental and body energies. In the short days of winter we miss these energising effects, and the inducement to rise early is not so strong in the winter as in the summer. There is no light to rouse us from the lethargic feeling engendered by a night's rest—to set the bodily and mental energies in motion. By way of compensation for the failure of the sun to stimulate us to wakefulness in the morning, the unbroken dark- ness of the sleep time in winter probably gives us a more complete and undisturbed night's rest than in summer.

* * * The Rev. J. F. Matthews' " meetings for men " continue to be very well attended and to arouse keen interest in true Christianity. Quite unusual attention was directed to the subject of Mr. Matthews' address on Thursday night, which was Why should I pray ?" ancl a running fire of questions was kept tip. The speaker argued that prayer was the natural means of communication and fellowship with the Eternal God and Father ; prayer was also an eminently rational act, and served the best interests of man's economy ; a third reason offered was that God answered prayer. Answers came inevitably. They were often personal, and psychological in character. Clarifying of the judgment, strengthening of the will, the passion for righteousness, were all increased as the result of praying. Was anyone bold enough to say that there were not answers to prayer ? * *

The Member for Wariington received a cordial welcome on Thursday when he appeared at the Liberal soiree after an all too long absence from the midst of his supporters. Mr. Crosfiehl is a popular man, and it has been a source of regret among Warrington Liberals that they have, owing to his ill-health and the pressure of business, seen so little of him of late. It was remarked both at the Lion Hotel and the Liberal Club that the Member was looking better, and it is to be hoped that he will have improved health in the future. Yesterday he attended the inaugural public meeting of the 'Warrington Garden Suburb scheme, and spoke warmly in favour of the proposals.

The —second of a series of meetings under the auspices of the Education Committee of the Warring- ton Co-operative Society will be held on Thursday in the Sankey-street Co-operative Hall, when a recital from memory of Charles Dickens' "Christmas Carol ' will be given by Mr. Barnish Barnsdale. The annual meeting of the members of the Warring- ton Savings Bank will be held on Tuesday week. Warrington music lovers will be pleased that the Musical Society have this year selected "The Messiah" for rendering at their second subscription concert. Handel's oratorio is ever popular and its presentation immediately before Christmas (December 22nd) is of course appropriate. The artistes at the concert will include Miss Gleeson White, saprano ; Miss Nellie Anderton, contralto ; Mr. Charles Saunders, tenor ; and Mr. Robert Radford, bass. Particular \attention is drawn to the popular prices which have been arranged for the concert which we are sure will be greatly appreciated. The plan for reserved seats will be opened to subscribers to-day and to non-sub- scribers on Wednesday. ' The annual gymnastic display in connection with the Borough Gymnasium will be held on Monday. A. popular feature of the evening's entertainment will be the exhibitions by Mr. Charles Wilson, champion all-round jumperof the world. On Tuesday evening a grand gymnastic display will be given in the Bold-street schoolroom by members of the St. Helens Y.M.C.A. Musical items will also be given by members of the Bold-street Choir. The quarterly meeting of the Warrington Trades- men's Association will be held at Messrs. Toft's Assembly Room on Tuesday evening. The subject for discussion at Monday's meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association is A social problem and how solved by taxing land values." The proceeds of the annual concert in connection with People's College, which will be held in the Parr Hall on December 20th,will be in aid of the Infirmary Extension Fund. An excellent programme has been arranged and the venture promises to be as great a success as ever. The prize distribution in connection with the School of Art,Secondary school and Technical institute will take place in the Parr Hall on Thursday. Sir Henry F. Hibbert, chairman of the Lancashire Educa- tion Committee will hand the prizes to the successful students. So great has been the demand for tickets that an early applieation is advisable. Whltecross Ward Vacancy. This vacancy, occasioned by the death of Councillor Walter Brough, has not been formerly declared and no candidates are yet in the field. Several gentlemen are being approached by the Liberal Ward Committee who at their last meeting placed on record their high appreciation of the late Councillor Brough's services and passed a vote of sympathy with the widow and family in their bereavement.
Licensing Changes. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Mr. J. E. L. Kinsley, Wilderspool-causeway, was granted temporary authority to sell at the Causeway Hotel, in lieu of Mr. Ephraim Aukland.

Taxation of Land Values. This reform was powerfully advocated at a meeting held in the Co-operative Hall last evening in connec- tion with the English League for the Taxation of Land Values. The principal speaker was Mr. McHugh, of Birkenhead, who dealt with the subject in an able and interesting manner.

div.head: Technical Scholars at Messrs. Crosfield's
div.p: Technical Scholars at Messrs. Crosfield's

On Wednesday —evening between 80 and 100 of the senior boys and girls from the Technical School paid a visit to Messrs. Crosfield's works at Bank Quay at tle invitation of the directors and were shown the interesting processes of soap-making and its allied chemistry. Afterwards the young visitors were enter- tamed to tea by the firm, and heard an address from Captain G-. R. Crosfield on the ideals of the National Service League. Captain Crosheld advised the boys to join the League and offered the use of the Appleton rifle range. He humorously advised the girls to interest their sweethearts in the matter. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. Pig Dealer's Failure. •

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Ridgway, Thomas Parkinson appeared for his public examination. Debtor said he carried on the business of a pig dealer at Orford. His failure was due to losses through the deaths of pigs and to r law costs. He admitted that he had given a bill of , sale to his brother which practically covered the whole of his assets, but he never thought the bill would be put into operation and hoped he would be able to recover his position. His liabilities were .QIG ss. 2d. and assets .-Zl3 17s. The examination was closed.

Alderman Bolton's Present to the Queen. Atttongst the presents received by the Queen on Saturday was a large box of beautiful orchids sent by Alderman Bolton, and the flowers were highly appreciated.

-- Popular Penny Concert. There was again a large attendance at the popular penny concert in the Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday evening, when an admirable entertain- ment was provided. The items included pianoforte solos by Miss Lester, Mr. Platt. and Mr. Goeenough, the two latter being encored warmly for a duet. Miss G. Henshall pleased the audience with a violin solo. Several gramophone selections were supplied by Mr. Harold Silcock. Mr. Alfred Grounds scored a great success with his humorous items. The accompani- ments were played by Mrs. Foreman and Mr. Frank Hickman. St George's Mission.

On Sunday at the conclusion of the evening service, an interesting presentation took place, the members of the choir and teachers presenting Miss Sanson with an engraved silver tea pot and jam dish on the occasion of her marriage. In the absence of the Curate-in-charge, the Rector kindly consented to make the presentation, and in doing so said how thankful he was to Miss Sanson for the services she had rendered to the Mission both as a teacher and a mem- ber of the choir. He hoped that her married life would be even happier than her single life and he assured her that it was a great pleasure to the teachers and members of the choir to make her the present they had done to mark their appreciation of her kind services. Miss Sanson briefly thanked the subscribers.

TABLE, FLOOR, AND HANGING LAMPS in large variety. Lstest patterns.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- monger Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. National Service League. A meeting of the honorary helpers of the Warring- ton Branch of the National Service League was held at 7.30 p.m., at the Lion Hotel on Monday. Present : Capt. Crosfield, Messrs. Ball, Clarke, Elwell, Gimson, Gallon, Harris, Houghton, Hampson, Owen an' Dr. Ormandy. The arrangements for the meeting on December .18th at the Brick-street Mission were discussed. The speakers for this meeting are Mr. Holden the hon. secretary of the Bolton Branch, and Mr. G. Holman Kingdon. They will deal with the question of national training from the working man's point of view and show that it would prove a grand holiday impossible to obtain by any other means. They will deal too with the enhanced value of a man because of the lessons in order method &c., taught in military training. Ancient Order of Foresters. A dinner and social in connection with the War- rington District Past Officers Society took piaci:Oat the Masons Arms, on Saturday last, when 40 officers had an excellent dinner, and the social was a most success- ful one. Miss Bancroft rendered three well received songs, and Mr. P. Bradford was thoroughly appreciated in his wonderful conjuring and illusionist tricks. Mr. Percy Hignett acted as accompanist and humorist. During the evening; District Secretary Bro. Davies presented an illuminated address and emblematical sash to Past District Chief Ranger Bro. Peter Pesicock who is chairman of the Society. He pointed out that Bro. Peacock had worked very hard, and enthusi- astically in the interests of Friendly Societies, and the Foresters in particular, during the last ten years, and the recognition was one which the whole of the members knew was well earned. Several P.D.C.R.'s spoke in praise of Bro. Peacock's work, and afterwards P.D.C.R. Bro. G. Maybury presented Bro. Wilding of the second Order with a framed emblem for his services as Chairman of Sanctuary Mercy Court Na. 210, which position he has held 18 months. Suitable replies were given by Bros. Peacick and Wilding.—The toast of the Warrington District was given by P.D.C.R. Bro. Chrimes, and replied to by P.D.C.R. Bro. H. Maybury.

PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. " A History of Discovery in Flame." This was the title of an interesting lecture delivered at the works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, on Wednesday evening by Mr. W. Roscoe Hardwick, B.Sc., secretary of the Liverpool Branch of the Society of Chemical Industry. Notwithstanding the wretched weather, there was a good attendance of employees of the firm and other townspeople interested in the subject. Mr. Hardwick is an exceptionally able lecturer and held the close attention of his audience throughout. He emphasised the importance of the subject by pointing out that we were dependent, if not for our very existence at least for many of our, comfort upon flame in its modified form. Referring to some of the latest dis- coveries, he pointed out that the researches of a. German\ professor had had such important results that Germany need no longer ba dependent upon the good will of this country for the supply of explosives for use in war. He proceeded to trace the progress of scientific knowledge in regard to flama and its pros- perties, the lecture being copiously illustrated with experiments and lantern slides. A. unique series of photographs of petroleum wells which had got beyond control and were sending forth great columns of flame, were thrown upon the screen—The lecturer was cordially thanked on the proposition of Dr. Markel.

International Trade. • International trade formed the subject of ,an interesting . address which was delivered by Mr. Philips, of Liverpool, at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association on Monday. There was a fair attendance, bver which Mr. H. Gray presided. The Lecturer quoted figures as to the trade of the leading nations of the world in which one striking factor - that in all cases but three imports exceeded exports—was noticeable. Perhaps the most persistent cry which had been heard of late years was that because a country was apparently sending more out in value than it imported it was necessarily pros- perous. Tjiat was a fallacy and it was not new. In sticking a nation's balance sheet regard must be paid. to the invisible exports which, though finding no record in official figures, were a mighty force in the nation's activity. To fake the most important item—shipping—the United Kingdom claimed 50 per cent. of the world's trade and to that must be added foreign investments With a population ,equal to France we were doing an export trade of £130,000,000 more, with 20,000,000, fewer inhabitants than Germany £.60,000,000 more, and with half of the population of the United States of America were doing an equal export trade. Those figures were eloquent and showed that not only was John Bull prosperous but that his customers were , doing well. Let us not hope for or do anything to influence the dimination of our trade with other nations or of one nation with another. The greater the trade and mutual dependence the greater the , guarantee of peace so therefore let England do all she could to foster the increase Of wealth in other countries,believing and knowing that she would share in that prbsperty and maintain her position as one of the greatest trading nations. (Applause.) —An linteresting discussion followed at the close of which the lecturer was heartily thanked for his address.

Picture. Exhibition at the Academy.

An exhibition of pictures and other Works of art is being held at the Old Academy and closes to-day (Saturday). Interest attaches to the various exhibits inasmuch as they are the work of the follmving local ladies and gentlemen : Miss Broadbent, Miss Dakin, Mr. H. C. Carter, Miss H. Fairclough, Mrs. Fleming, Miss Fletcher, Miss Pickavance, Miss C. Sloane, Miss Waring, and Mr. H. Woodier. Most of the pictures are water-colour drswings chiefly of the impressionist type, depicting landscapes, though there are some oil-paintings, and several figure- studies, interiors, criir. Miss Fletcher's specimen of work on porcelain,and Miss Dakin's miniatures may per- haps without invidiemsness be mentioned as especially meritorious. A visit to the exhibition—admission to ' which is gratis—can be strongly recommended while there is yet opportunity. Bankruptcy Follows Litigation. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Ridgway, Noah Ruben appeared for his public examination. Debtor said he commenced busi- ness in Knutsford-road Warrington, as a picture framer &ic., without any capital. In November 1905 he was severely injured by a motor car colliding with him whilst he was riding a bicycle on Wilderspool-road and prevented from attending business for jour months. During this period he had to pay a man .£.2 10s. a week to manage the business. The owners of the motor car offered him £3O compensation, but lie refused to accept this, and sued them for £lOO damages. He lost his case and was involved in costs which be was unable to meet, and had to file his petition. His liabilities were £ll4 2s. 9d., and assets 4]o. The examination was closed.

The Late Councillor Brough, On Sunday evening there was a large congregation at the Padgate Wesleyan Church on the occasion of a special memorial service for the late Councillor Brough. The service was of a most impressive char- Ater, and was conducted by the Rev. Wm. Mellor, who preached from St. Matthew xvii. 5, "While be yet spire, behold a bright cloud overshadowed them." In referring to the deceased, the preacher said they had met that evening under a cloud, but it was not a dark cloud. Remembering all that Mr. Brough was in his bright and consistent Christian character, and in his varied services to the church and to the town, they had a keen sense of loss, and they mourned not for him who had been removed from their midst, but for themselves who were so greatly bereaved. The cloud which overshadowed them was brightened by Christian faith and hope, for their friend had entered upon the rest and reward of the good and faithful. He prayed that they might all profit by the good example which had been left them, and that those whom this great loss most closely touched might be strengthened in their trial. Appropriate voluntaries were played by Mr. Hugh Mellor. UNDER THE CLocx for Good Boo Ts. Advt.—

Widow's Suicide. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at his Court at the Police Station, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of Louisa Wardle Stirrup (widow of the late Edward Stirrup, fitter's labourer), who committed suicide by drinking carbolic acid at the residence of her sister, 'Sipa Smith, of 22, Dannett-street, on Saturday. Dr. Smith stated that he was called in to see Mr. Stirrup, who was lying on the bed in a state of unconscious- ness, and breathing in a very laboured manner. She was evidently dying, and be considered the case hope- less. He saw an empty bottle which had contained strong carbolic acid, and a jug which had in it about half a spoonful. Parts of the woman's body had been burnt by the acid. —Myra Smith, widow, said the deceased, who was 45 years of age, was her sister and lived with her. On going upstairs shortly after half past ten she.discovered a strong smell of carbolic acid. Ths deceased was lying on the bed and was uncon- scious. She saw a bottle and a jug which contained , carbolic acid. She at once sent for Dr. Smith. Deceased had lost her husband a few months ago and had since been strange in her manner. Her sister had of late been drinking heavily. She had never heard ' her threaten to take away her life.—The jury returned la verdict to the effect that the deceased had committed Isuicide while temporarily insane.

The Henry Taylor Fund A meeting of the subscribers to the above fund was held on Tuesday afternoon at the King's Cafe, Bridge- street, Mr. T. E. Gibson in the chair. Councillor Steel, (the hon. secretary) submitted the statements of accounts, which showed that the sum of £97 sa. 9d. had been subscribed, and that after deducting ..4.:13 expenses incurred in the funeral there was left a balance of £B3 us. 91 On the proposition of the Rev. J. Hirst, of Liverpool (Diocesan secretary of the Church of England Temperance Society), seconded by Mrs. Garnett, it was resolved that the Rtv. E. C. E. Carleton and Mr. Steel be appointed joint treasurers of the fund, and they were authorized to dispose of the money to the widow as they thought desirable. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the local newspapers for having advertised the fund and the meetings. and for having printed various matters connected with the appeal to the public. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from the Rev. James Davies, Mr. Talbot (chief constable), Mr. Jenkins and Mr. Draper.—Councillor Steel has received a letter from Mrs. ' Taylor in which she thanks the subscribers and workers in connection with the fund. " HERALD " KITCHEN RANGES and " Peveril " Fire Grates are hard to best.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt• Crosfields' Fire Brigade. On Saturday evening last the Recreation Room of Messrs. Crosfield's Fire Station was the scene of a very pleasant re-union when Chief Officer Gallon, his lieutenants, Messrs. Flood and Whitby, and the men of the Fire Brigade, over 50 in number, met for their fifth annual dinner. Dr. Markel who presided was supported by Captain Crosaeld and in addition Messrs. C. H. Kingdon P.nd W. H. R. Darlington were present as invited guests. After the dinner, which was quite exquisite in its way, the topt of "The King" was duly given from the chair and a most enjoyable "sing-song "followed. The programme, which was enriched by one or two excellent short stories from the guests, included a number of songs with cornet solos, items by a concertina quartette and by two quartettes of Crosfield's Band ,and some excellent recit- ations and "pitter-patter." Before taking his leave Dr. Markel said :" It has been whispered to me,by the way,l that you are anxious to have a billiard table here.l hope by when we next meet it will have been found possible to realise this wish." (Applause.) The evening's amusement was carried on after the depar- ture of the visitors to a late hour,and was in every way delightful. It may be said that a unique interest attaches to this dinner as being the first of its kind provided within the works entirely from the firm's resources. The Hall was tastefully and appro- priately decorated with flags and brigade trophies. The cooking was by the staff of the works dining rooms and everything from cutlery to cornet solos was home-furnished.

div.head: APPEAL CONCERT IN PARR HALL.
div.p: APPEAL CONCERT IN PARR HALL.

It was highly gratifying to find that the appeal con- cert held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening on behalf of the widow and family of the late Mr. James Fagan, of Orford-lane, met with such splendid support from the public. The object was a very deserving one, the facts of the case being extraordinarily sad. A representative committee had worked hard to ensure the success of the concert and they had their reward in seeing the hall filled to its utmost capacity. The pro- gramme was of more than usual interest, many well-known local artistes readily giving their services. Miss Carrie Hastings sang Tosti's "Gobd-bye" very feelingly and Miss Lily Boyle was heard to advantage in "II BaCCiO " (L. Arditi). One of the most enjoyable items of the evening was the dramatic recital The Uncle "which was given with fine power by Mr. W. Kilduff, the musical accompaniment being effectively played by Miss A. Kilduff. Miss Bessie Eckersley greatly pleased the audience with her inter- pretation of "A May morning" (Denza) and Miss Warren was also successful in the ever-popular " Kathleen Mavourneen " (Crouch). Mrs. John Dolan sang " Come back to Erin ' (Claribello) very acceptably azd Miss Lily Fairhurst had the honour Of 1 a recall for her expressive rendering of "On the banks of Allan water." (Horn). Miss Sexton did justice to that pretty song "Come sweet morning." Mr. J. Rabbitt is deservedly a favourite with Warring- ton audiences and his soulful interpretation of" Maid of Athens " (Allen) delighted the audience and called forth a vigorous encore. Other successful vocal solos were" Thy sentinel am I " (Watson) by Mr. J. Higham and" Queen of Love " (St. Quentin and" Lotus Land,' (Sidney Jones) by Mr. F. Warburton. The Lyric Quartette (Miss Woodland, Miss Fairhurst, Messrs. R. W. Cook and P. George) sang Killarney" and" God is a spirit," with great feeling, the voices blending beautifully. A quartette party from the Musical Society (Mrs. Booth, Miss Mabel Henshall, Messrs. J. Rabbitt and J.W.Bibby) contributed one of the gems of the evening, in the charming mardigal "Brightly dawns our wedding day " from the " Mikado." Instrumental quartettes by Messrs. Winstanley, J. Newns, D. Wilcocks and L. Gillooly acre creditably played and proved popular. The Apollo Choir maintained their high reputation with finished vocalisations of "The village blacksmith" and " To Ceclia" and were vociferously re- called. Mr. W. Woodcock conducted. The humorous element was supplied by Mr. Alfred Grounds and Mr. J. Emson who succeeded in creating uproarious mirth. Mr. W.H. Payton, Mus. Bac., ably discharged the duties of accompanist. It may he stated that the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst) showed their interest in the effort by attending. During and interval Councillor Toole (chairman of the committee) warmly thanked all who bad assisted.
