div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. H. AND MRS. DUNNICO.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. H. AND MRS. DUNNICO.
Social at Warrington.

The Rev. H.and Mrs.Dunnico renewed their acquaint- ance with Warrington on Monday when they were entertained at a social which was held in Atkinson's Cafe Bridge-street. The gathering was attended by members of the Rev. H. Dunnico's old congregation at Golborne-street Baptist Church and by some of those who had been in the habit of attending his Sunday evening services at the Parr Hall. After games and conversation a short meeting was held.presided over by Mr. Heywood. The principal item in the proceedings was the presentation of a framed photograph of the members of Golborne-street Chapel. to the Rev. H. Dunnico. The presentation was made by Miss Paul. The Rev. H. Durxmco, in reply, spoke of his deep love for his old friends at the church, and at the Parr Hall services, and said it was his plain speaking that induced the criticism of those who ought to have been his friends, and the hostility of those whose interests be attacked. Of all the clannish towns he had ever visited Warrington was the most clannish. The people kept their hearts and pockets closed until they got to know a man. The experience of every minister who had ever been to Warrington was that it was the hardest possible town to work in ; yet the people understood him. It was said he bad made enemies. He wanted to do so. The man who did not make enemies was not worth looking at. (Hear, hear and applause.) If he had had a trust deed broad and Christian enough on which he could have built up a broad church Liverpool would not have taken him from Warrington. He felt under the conditions existing in Warrington that he could not build up a Christian church after his own heart. Had the way been open for him to have remained in Warrington he would have done so, and, therefore, when the call .to Liverpool came he accepted it and be could assure them that he was happy in his work in that great city. (Applause.) Alluding to some remarks which had been jocularly made by one or two of the speakers about Mr. Dunnico eventually undertaking a pastorate in America, the Rev. gentleman said that if he left the Christian ministry it would be to enter Parliament ass Socialist. (Applause.) He had not the slightest bitterness against any man in Warrington. He bad met a large number of friends on his way from the station anxious to shake hands with him, and he had not fully realized until now how the people loved him. He thanked his friends for the portraits presented to him, and all of them for their kindness to him while in Warrington. (Applause.) Then followed an interval for refreshments, after which one of the ladies presented Nlrs. Dunnico with a very handsome bouquet. Songs were given by Mr. and Mrs. Hannan and Miss Hankey and pianofoate solos by Mrs. Foreman and Miss M. Hankey. Mr. J. Elwell and IMr. W. H. Wilson carried out the arrangements for the evening in a very satisfactory manner.

div.head: Farnborough _Boys' Band at WaiTington.
div.p: Farnborough _Boys' Band at WaiTington.

The boys' band and choir of the Farn—horough Branch of the children's homes founded by Dr. Stevenson, visited Wartington on Wednesday when they gave a concert in the Parr Hall. Owing to the inclement state of the weather there was only a small attendance over which the Mayor presided. At the outset his Worship warmly eulogised the work of the homes which he said had pr. ,ved and were continuing to prove a great blessing. The programme opened with Rossini's " Tancredi " which was almost faultlessly rendered by the band. Youthful as the performers were they displayed a remarkable command over the various instruments and proved that they have well earned the title of the best boys' band in the country which was given to them this year when they won the premier prize at the national contest in London. Other items were rendered with equal success during the evening, whilst the boys proved their versatility by interspersing with the instrumental music action songs and choruses. They also gave a very creditable musical drill. During anl interval the Rev. Bevan Shepherd, M.A., Vice-Principal of the Homes, delivered an address and made an earnest appeal for financial assistance. He pointed out that the cost of the Homes which are established in different centres of the country, was about £38,004) per annum, and was met by the free-will gifts of the people. One of the Homes was at present in course of construction at Frodsham and in January 1907 about 120 orphan children would be received there. The children would be taken irrespective of age, creed, or locality,and after a thorough training would be placed in situations.Mr.Shepherd gave an interesting descrip- tion of the work in the various establishments con- nected with the institution.

div.head: CHRISTMAS PRESENTS.
div.p: CHRISTMAS PRESENTS.

- - The London and North-Western Railway Company have made complete arrangements for the collection, quick transit and prompt delivery of Christmas parcels in all the principal towns on their system and all parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland. Special trains will be run and through vans will be attached to the principal passenger trains for the accommodation of the traffic and additional delivery arkd collection services by parcel yaps and carts between the receiving offices and the railway stations will be in operation during Christmas week. Senders are advised that as an extra precaution a duplicate address label should be enclosed in each parcel so that the name of the consigner may be ascer- tained in the event of the outside address becoming detached or defaced.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 8, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 8, 1906.
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. LANCASHIRE RUGBY CUP FINAL.

Ll3y " Ovalist."' Dire misfortune overtook the Warringtonians on Saturday at Wigan and dealt them a sorry blow. In the first five minutes of the final for the Lancashire Cup all the West Lancashire men's hopes were shattered and the issue made practically certain for the Rangers of Broughton. Fish's ill-luck on the Wigan ground has been often commented upon. Two years ago his collar-bone was broken in a County match, last season he sustained a serious injury to his leg, and on Saturday. he sustained a broken right arm the first time he handled the ball. A creel fate seems to have been dogging the Warrington skipper's foot- steps, but this was the worst blow of thelot. It threw a cloud over the game and plunged the 3,000 odd sup- porters of Wanington into the depths of despair. With the departure of such an accomplished player as Fish, Warrington's chances of scaring the Cup went also. Could anything have been more aggravating and unfortunate?

I might answer the question myself by saying that the next incident of the game was even more galling to the crowd, whose sympathies were in, the main with the Warrington men. 'Hardly had play been resumed when one of the Broughton backs took a pot-shot at goal. The ball was directed accurately, but fell unmistakably a couple of feet tinder the bar. Referee Smith immediately signalled a goal amid a et= of hoots and groans and the excited protests of the Warrington players. I suppose Mr. Smith made one of those fatal errors which he seems to reserve for important occasions. Certainly his experiences as referee when Warrington have been in a cup final have been unfor- tunate for Warrington. There is often a doubt about • the legitimacy of a point in football under both codes, but so far 1 have not met anyone who had a doubt about this goal. Everybody who was in a position to see is unanimous that the ball passed well under the bar, and personally I would stake my oath upon the fact. This incident, coming immediately after Fish's injury was enough to dishearten any team, but the Warrington men pulled themselves together and pre- sented a bold front to the Broughton attack.

Their misfortunes were not at an end, however. Some ten minutes later Berry, the fall back, was stunned in a collision with one of the Broughton forwards and while be was lying on the ground injured, Wilson scored a try after knocking on a couple of yards in a manner which looked more deliberate than accidental. If the Referee had seen Berry lying unconscious he ought to have stopped the game before Wilson got the ball. For a time Warrington were reduced to *eying with four forwards, but on Berry's return the remaining five put a better complexion on matters and the Rangers were unable to add to their lead before the interval, when the score was a goal and a try to nil.

The story of the second half is soon told. Broughton got a couple of scrappy tries and a goal from a mark and one from a pemilty. The first try was the result of a scramble on the line after Hogg had missed an easy pass and knocked on, while the second was due to a mistake by the Warrington full back. Berry tried to kick the ball dead but only sent it over the goal line for Flynn to drop on unopposed. Warrington,wbo had been playing with unflagging energy and pluck all through finished up with a rattle, and received some reward for .their pains and penalties. Dickenson scored the beat try of the match after pretty combina- tion with Hockenhall and Thomas, and just on time Brooks took a pass from Lees and dashed over with a try which crowned a good afternoon's work for the right-winger. Preston had several shots at goal, but none were easy, and the ball generally just avoided the posts by a foot or two. The total score was there- fore 15 points to 6 points, but many people thought Warrington's six were worth nearly all the lot which fell to the lucky Rangers.

Under the difficult circumstances they had to face Warrington undoubtedly played a very fine uphill game. They never lost heart and were slways too dangerous for the Rangers to indulge in any slack- ness. Considering the extra man they had in the scrummage the Rangers forwards never got much advantage over the Warrington five, who gave a magnificent exhibition. The backs on both sides were well matched with,if anything a slight superiority for Warrington. Had Fish been in his accustomed place I thing theresult would have been far different. As things were the team was nearly equal to winning the match with an average amount of luck. But the luck was all the other way.

Diekenson played a superior centre game to Wilson, the latter's play being chiefly remarkable for long well-judged punting. In fact he taught a lesson in the art of finding touch under the present rules, but rather over-did the part. Brooks was the best wing on the field and it was the hardest " lines " imaginable that he did not equalise the points with the great effort he made in the first half. Hogg was certainly the worst wing and could never get past Thomas, who filled Fish's place with distinct credit Berry and Taylor both played below form and were uncertain in their catching. There was a sort of duel between the respective full backs—both young players—and Barlow, the Broughton man, took all the honours. His display was well-nigh perfect. Berry still waits for the bounce to often. The two best halves were Lees and Flynn, but the half-back play on either side was not very classy.

The game was a very good one to watch, being brimful of lively passages. There was just a little too much kicking, and considering the reputation the Rangers' backs have for combination their display was distinctly moderate. But for Brooks' thrilling runs and Dickinson's great centre display, the backs would have had to play second fiddle to the forwards. The two packs contained some of the most finished exponents in the Union, and men like Preston, Board- man, Beetham and Ruddick were always conspicuous.

Warrington will be sadly in need of a left wing for a couple of months at least. Fish sustained a fracture of both bones in the forearm and there is only the emergency man, Jordan, to fall back upon. The latter is a most useful player and might make a second Brooks with steady practice and coaching, but a speedier man is certainly required. Now is the time for the Committee to distinguish themselves by a grand coup. I know of several good wings : Williams, Loubser, Stegmann, Simpson and the like. The Committee may know of others more approachable Just now the reserves are badly off for speedy men.

There was a mistake in most of the papers on Monday in the repo ts of Saturday's matches. Runcorn's visit to Rochdale was only in the nature o a "friendly "and should not have been included inf the League table. The "Linnets " ought to have played Broughton, and this fixture was completed on Wednesday when the League leaders had to bow the knee to the Lancashire cup-holder to the tune of lo points to 3 points The re-played match between Oldham and Salford took place on Monday when Oldham reversed the previous result by scoring 10 points to G points, The "Reds " have thus lost two valuable points through their " kit " going astray prior to the previous unfinished encounter. It will be remembered that they were beating Oldeam 7-0 on that occasion/when darkness closed the proceedings The following is the League Table up-to-date For Agst. Per. , _ _

Warrington have dropped a place or Ova, but their point average is still one of the best in the League. No club has had its line crossed on so few occasions, while the points " for " will take some equalling by clubs who have not yet had their fill out of Liverpool.

To-day, Warrington are again due at that abode of ill-luck, the Wigan ground, this time in an ordinary League match with the Wiganers. One cannot feel very hopeful under all the circumstances, but on Wigan's present form there should bs a chanca for the Warrington men. The visiting ,tam will be pretty nearly the same as last week, Hockenhall taking Fish's place aild Jordan going to half-back. with Lees, while Shugars comes in for Harmer, who got rather knocked about in. the Cup final. The team is therefore : Berry, full back; Hockenhall, Dickinson, Taylor and Brooks, threequarters - Lees and Jordan, half-backs ; Boardman, Preston, homes, Heath, Naylor, and Shugars, forwards.

There will be a rare struggle between the respec- tive" A" teams at Warrington, for both are running neck and neck for the Championship. Wigan beat the Warrington men by a norrow margin at Wigan a few weeks ago, but I fully expect the locals will be amply avenged to-day. They have got a powerful side out, particularly forward, viz :—Knight. Landot, Cartwright, Davies and Jones; Jenkins and Kay ; Belton, Jolley, Forster, Bradshaw, Boardman and Holbrook.

• Warrington's two matches with Liverpool City have been re-arranged and will both take place this month The match at Liverpool will be played on Monday next, and the return on December 26th. The War- rington men ought to manage to raise their aggregate score to over 30 points this week and thus be the first team to do so in Northern Loagua football before Christmas.

Hockey. On Saturday last Stockton Heath visited Western and scored an easy victory by 9 goals to 4. The ground was very swampy and hardly suitable for the short passing gaale played by the Stockton Heath forwards, otherwise a cricket score would have been run up. In justice to the Western club it must be said that they were minas four of their regular players. The goals for Stockton Heath were scored by S. Baxter 3, W. H. Banks 3 and W. Richardson 3.

On the Stockton Heath side, the three inside for- wards played very well, at times.simply racing through the opposing defence as if they had been off the field, still we should like to see Baxter combine more, though one must admit he does some very fine pieces of indiviaual play.

AB predicted in these columns the COunty Committee have been forced to recognize the sterling merits of W. H. Banks, the Stockton Heath centre forward. Banks has been chosen to represent Lancashire at Lincoln on December 13th. We hope he will find it convenient to make the journey, and that he will pro- duce his best form.

The'Second Eleven match at Arpley was of a very disappointing nature. Owing to unavoidable circum- stances the home side turned out two men short. Ah oould only be expected the result was never in doubt, the final score reading : Western 5, Stockton Heath 0.
This week Stockton Heath play New Brighton Wanderers Ist and 2nd elevens; the following teams have been chosen to represent Stockton Heath :

Ist (away) :—F. G. Kertland (goal) E. E. Woods and R. Hallows (backs) G. G. Hatton. A. H. Rathbone and E. Pierpoint (halves), H. Dolan, W. Richardson, W. H. Banks, S. Baxter and Eric Fairclough (forwards). Train leaves Central Station 12.50. Referee :—W. Carter.

- 2nd (On Alpley Ground) C. S. Woods (goal). P. B. Hawtin and B. Silcock (backs), H. W. Guest, J. Houghton and 0. M. de Jong (halves, C. S. Smith, T. H. Owen, C. W. Walker, W. Linnel and A. Hodgkinson, (forwards) N. W. Bellamy referee : bully off 2.30.

div.head: LIBERAL SOIREE.
div.p: LIBERAL SOIREE.
Successful Gathering at the Lion Hote .
Visit of Mr. A. H. Crosfield

I On Thursday evening a most enjoyable soiree, pro meted by the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion, was held in the Lion Hotel. There were about I 130 people present —just the required number to givel a brightness to,the scene and yet allow sufficient room, for everyone's comfort and enjoyment. Among those present wers the Member for the Borough, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Mr. Charles E. Parker (President of the Liberal Association) and Mrs. Parker. Last winter the corresponding event took the form of a dance only, but on Thursday night there was much more variety in, the proceedings and in consequence both the young and the middle-aged found plenty of pleasing occupation. The main event, in the I , first half of the proceedings, was a whist- drive held in the Assembly Room, and there were about 100 contestants for the six handsome prizes I I which had been provided by the generosity of Mrs. I Armitage and Mr.Crosfield.Twenty games were played in about two hours, and while it was impossible even for the most thoughtful committee to provide that everybody should have good "hands," all enjoyed' the quiet contest for supremacy. At the same time, in an adjoining room, Mrs. Parker, assisted by Miss Walker, organised a number of lively " parlour " games for the non-whist players and everythinghere went as merry as a marriage bell, prizes being awarded to the most expert players. A little incidental music was also provided by Mrs. Parker and Mrs. Dow, of Eccles. At 10.30 p.m. there was a break in the pro- ceedings for the purposes of refreshment, and the two rooms available were soon thronged by people anxious to partake of the good things Mr. Lee had provided. Meanwhile, the by no means light task of checking the whist scores had been performed, and after supper the prizes were presented to the winners by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. Then followed dancing until 2 a.m. to the strains of Mr. J. T. Barton's excellent orchestra which, it should be added, had played instrumental selections at intervals while tbe whist drive was in progress. The winners of the whist prizes were as follows : Ladies : 1, Mrs. Page, 147 ; 2, Mrs. White, 145 ; consolation prize, Mrs. O'Brien, 108. Gentlemen : 1, Mr. J. Hallitvell, 166 ; 2, Mr. J. J. Pritchard, 149 ; consolation prize, Mr. J. Rymer Young, 111. In making the presentation, Mr. CROSFIELD said lie was pleased to tell the co m • pany that there was to be no speech-making. No one was more happy on that account than he—although perhaps he ought not to say so—coming, as he did, straight from the home of that particular kind of oratory which Mr. Labauchere once told him never 'failed to sooth him into pleasant slumber. (Laughter.) He was sure it would be a great mistake if he attempted to sooth anyone in that way on such a festive occasion ; and although he believed on another evening he would lave to perform the duty —which was one of the pleasant duties which fell to the lot of everyone in his position—of answering for those things which he had done and which he ought not to have done, and for those things which he had left undone and that he ought to have done —(laughter) —he was not going to trespass on their patience or kindness with any explanation of the kind that night and he hoped they would forgive him for postponing it. (Hear hear.) _ _

The M.C.'s for the evening were Messrs., C. E. Parker, PC. Garnett, and E. V. Walker, while the committee which had arranged the soirde was com- posed of Mrs. Parker, Mrs. Lindley, Mrs.P.' C. Garnett, Miss Guest, Mrs. Osborne (secretary), Mrs. Walker (treasurer), and Messrs. P. C. Garnett, and E. V. Walker. The Lion Hotel rooms had been tastefully decorated for the occasion by Messrs. G. and J. Weaver.

Warrington Rural District Council. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Conncil was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday when there were present: —Dr.Murray (pre- siding),Messrs.G. Mather,G.Thompson,J. W. Knowles, W. Houghton, R. Forsha,w, J. Ball, J. C. Sutton (clerk), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Barnage (assistant surveyor) and Dr. Sephton (medical officer). —Dr. Sephton reported that during the month there had been 22 births and 21 deaths. The death rate was equal to 21 per 1,000, as against 26, tk average of the past three months, and 31.3 for the corresponding period of last year. Eleven of the deaths occurred in the County Asylum, Winvrick, exclusive of which the death rate proper for the district was equal to 10'00 Per /,000. Seven cases of scarlet fever had been notified.— The Surveyor sub- mitted ths amenned plans and schemes from Mr. Compton Hall for the improvement of Spittle Bridge. Mr. Hall's total estimate for the larger scheme is £3,805 2s. 5d., amended smaller scheme £1,053 3s. 10d. It was dectded to enter upon negotiations with a view to crrrying out the larger scheme.
Richard Buckham (20), the young Essex labourer, suffered the last dread penalty of the law at Chelmsford on Tuesday for the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Watson at Basildon.

div.head: TELL -COOK.
div.p: TELL -COOK.

Just as our home-farmers watch the weather during the weeks of harvest, so the Grecian currant-grower, whose financial interests are wholly centred in the 'Currant, watches anxiously for the signs of those fierce rains whioh sometimes sweep over wide tracts of the currant country, rui sing the ripening fruit. Home-cooks may be extremely glad that this year's currant crop, though somewhat shorter than usual, is of excellent quality. Currants are undoubtedly a most inexpensive and nutritious food, exceptionally good for growing children and healthful for young and old alike. That capital little book—" Currants : A Few Tasty Recipes,"—is proving a very real help to thousands of housewives who have, for months past, been enquiring for just such an aid to everyday cookery of the Currant. Ask your grocer to-day for this most useful and interest- ing booklet. It will be given you free.

div.head: MESSRS. TUCK'S XMAS CARDS.
div.p: MESSRS. TUCK'S XMAS CARDS.

With thoughts of "Glad Tidings" come Messrs. Raphael Tuck's annual reminder of "a good time coming," and among the dainties peculiar to Xmas none please moresthan the publications from Raphael Rouse. What with Calendars, Booklets, Xmas Cards, and the übiquitous "cc.," one is bewildered with an array of artistic novelties. To particularize would be a task, to select would be a pleasure, feeling that whether for old or young, grave or gay, one's wishes stud taste would be appealed to. There is nothing to offend the eye, or sense of the fitness of things; all is artistic, harmonious, and perfectly filched. We commend these "annuals" to our readers 'with every confidence in their power to incrense the apacity fo. "A Merry Xmas" for themselves and oheir friends.

—There is one feature of Messra.Tuck's publications this Tear to which we ought to draw special attention, as it is quite unique. We refer to the "Art Portfolio Calendars" (Patented), a series of•designs in a portfolio frame through which the pictures are seen. We prophesy for these striking and beautiful productions an unprecedented success. Father Tuck's famous " annual" has been doubled in size at the original price, and the post-card competition is approaching mammoth proportions with £6,686 in prizes.
The Pope has written an autograph letter to the King of Biotin pointing out the dangers threatening the monarchy should the anti-Catholic policy of the Government be continued. _

A fire in the upper p trt of the warebo Ise of Smith, Sons, and Lagghland in Mitchell-street, Glasgow, on Tuesday, did damage estimated at from .£B,OOO to £lO,OOO. "Bridges " were brought into use for the hoses, so as not to interfere with the tram service.

The unique healing powers of Zam-Buk having established it as the standard "first-aid" for home use, the following carefully-compiled hints on the proper treatment of common injuries will prove useful to housewife, mother, and bread-winner alike : GENERAL—The family box of Zarn-Litik should be always on a handy shelf, where even the children can get at it if mother isn't around to bind up the bleeding anger or scarred knee. Clean lint ore surgical bandage (to he bought for a copper) will also prove useful. The importance of perfect cleanliness cannot be over- estimated. Bear in mind ; (1) that the hands should be carefully washed before applying Zam-Bnk ; (2) to always use clean rags, and burn old ones; (3) to keep your box of Zam-Buk covered, and never to put any back into the box after a dressing. CUTS.—Rinse with cold water and bind up tightly with clean linen,on which Zam-Buk has been generously smeared. When bleeding has stopped the bandage may be loosened. When dressing for a second time with Zam-Bnk, which should be in a few hoits, the edges of the wound may be pressed together gently. JAGGED CUTS. SCRAPES, &C.—Wash carefully in tepid water with soft, clean rag, and apply Zam-Buk as for cuts.

SCALP WOUNDS.-Cut away hair, clean thoroughly, and apply Zam-Buk thickly. In a few minutes, when bleeding has ceased, remove any watery exudation and cover neatly with thin •plaster stretched across the wound.

_ BRUISES.—AppIy Zam-Buk, and rub well in, rubbing only one way—towards the body. This will lessen the swelling, soothe the pain, prevent discoloration, and ensure the speedy restoration of healthy skin. BURNS AND SCALDS.—AppIy Zam-Buk with the least 'possible delay, the exclusion of air being of the first importance. Apply the balm direct to the wound, or spread first on stips of lint after the lint, place a layer or two of cotton wool and then bandage carefully so that the dressing remains in place. Dressings with Zam-Buk should be reptiated once a day ; or oftener if thought necessary. With the use of Zam-Buk pain is subdued, inflammation and festering averted, and a new layer of skin is quickly formed. SPRAINS.—In serious cases foment to reduce swelling then rub Zam-Buk in, gently but persistently, for several minutes, afterwards bandaging firmly but not tightly. The bandage should support the joint, but not interfere with the circulation. A few days' rest is 11 that should be necessary in the average case, and then a little movement may be encouraged to guard against stiffness. If fresh applications of Zam-Buk be rubbed in vigorously with the end of a soft towel, the whole of the ligaments and muscles will become considerably strengthened, and the joint quite sound again. There is no preparation which is so unique and so unfailingly successful as Zam-Buk. Of all chemists, Is. Id. per box, or 2s. Pd. for larger size, preferred for family use as it contains nearly four times the quantity.

div.head: AN ANECDOTE OF COMMODORE DEWK
div.p: AN ANECDOTE OF COMMODORE DEWK

MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS, Many thanks for this week's post. It has taken me just about double the time to get through. What with letters and contribu- tions from new members, Christmas riddles from others applications for bottles of Mason's Extract, and a hundred-and-one other things, my time has been completely taken up. Now there is one thing I intended to mention in my last week's letter, but quite forgot, and that is—All those dear members who have been send- ing in contributions for the Christmas column, and have seen no notice of them, must not think they were of no good; but, to tell the truth, I am keeping them all back in A big envelope until the proper time. Beside', it would not do to say who had won prizes now. If I did—well, you wouldn't like to 14 kept waiting until Cl}ristmas, would you? _ .

So far as the usual weekly prizes go, I have awarded them this week to Annie Rowland, who contributes "Santa Claus and the Mouse," and to R. Oldknow, for "An Anecdote of Commodore Dewey." Upon looking over a lot of contributions that I have received in the past, I came across a story, entitled, "Lost and Found"; but the letter has got separated from it, and there is no address on the back, sO I really don't know who kindly suit it in. If the 'owner happens to catch sight of Allis, and will send me on his or her name and address lie or she (whichever it is) will bear of something to his or her advantage.

I hope all my nephews who have seen Man's advertisements in all the papers will do their best to secure one of the six footballs they are offering free each week, for the best thing in the' way of a joke, conundrum, poetry, etc., sent in on a postcard. There's no zarm in trying, because, anyway, you get a x.ciaple of their really delicious Wine Essence,
If any of you boys happen to get tene, don't forget to drop a line announcing the faat.t.-: UNcLE NE)).
Dear Uncle Ned,—l have read the "Children's Corner" for' a long time, and- I thought I should like to join it. I am sending a piece of poetry, which I hope you will like. It is called:
THE GIANT AND THE DWARF. Is on through We's journey we go day by day, There are two whom we meet at each turn of
the way. To help or to hinder, to bless or to ban; And the names of these two are—"l Can't,"
and "I Can." I Can't " is a coward, half fainting with fright; At the first thought of peril, he slinks out of
sight; Skulks and hides, till the noise of the battle

is past, Or sells his best friends, and turns traitor at last. "I Can" is a hero, the first in the field; Though others may falter, he never will yield. He makes the long marches, he deals the last blow; His charge is the whirlwind that scatters the foe.
Then up and be doing! the day is not long; Throw fear to the winds, be patient and strong; Stand fast in your place, act your part like a
And when dtity calls, answer promptly, "1 Can." From your loving niece,
AMY GOMER.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l hope you are quite well. I have not written to you for a long time. I am sending you a nice piece, which I hope you will like. It is called:
SANTA CLAUS AND THE MOUSE.

One Christmas eve, when. Santa Claus Came to a certain house, To fill the children's stockings there, He fodnd a little mouse. "A merry Christmas, little friend," Said Santa Claus, so kind; "The same to you, sir," said the mouse; "I thought you wouldn't mind, If I should stay awake to-night, And watch you for a while." " You're very welcome, little friend," Said Santa, with a smile. And then to fill the stockings up, Before the mouse could 'wink, From toe to top, from top to toe, There wasn't left a chink. "Now they won't hold another thing," Said Santa Claus, with pride. A twinkle came in mouse's eyes, But humbly he replied: "It's• not polite to say it, and Your pardon I implore, But in the fullest stockings there I could put one thing more." Oh, oh!" said Santa, "silly mouse! - -

Don't I know how to pack? By tilling stockings all these years, should have learned the knack." And then he took the stocking down From where it hung so high, And said, "Now put in one thing more; • I give you leave to try."
A sailor in the cruiser "Boston," who w present at the battle of Manila Bay, fells ti following story:— The most affecting incident that occurs during the battle of Manila Bay, and which

all I the sa-ilors will remember through their lives, was the action of a powder-boy., These boys act as aides to captains and lieutenants in carrying mespges and doing errands. When the order was given to strip for action, one of the boys tore off his coat somewhat hurriedly, and it fell from his hands and went over the rail. down \into the water. A few moments before he had been gazing on his mother's photograph and just before he took his coat off he had \ kissed the picture and put it in his inside pocket. When the coat fell overboard, he turned to the captain and asked permission to get it. Naturally the request was refused. The boy then went to the other side of the ship, climbed down a ladder, swam round to the place where' the coat had dropped, and quickly succeeded in recovering it. When he came back, he was ordered in chains for disobedience. After the battle, he was tried by a court-martial for dis- obedience and found guilty. Commcdore Dewey became interested in the case, for he wondered why the boy, for the sake of ,an cad coat had risked his life by disobeying orders. The lad never told what his motives were. But when the Commodore talked to him in a kindly way, and asked him wily he had dote such strange things for an old coat,lie broke into tears, and told the commander that his mother's picture was in the coat. Commodore Dewey's eyes filled with tears as he listened io the story. Then he picked tht boy up in his arms and embraced him. He ordered the little fellow to be instantly released and pardoned. "Boys who love their mothers enough to risk their lives for their pictures shall not be kept in irons on this fleet,' he said.

Hoping I shall rife my story in prt, and will you kindly send me a bottle of Mason's Extract of Herbs, as saw in the " Gazette 7 that you had a d4ten (ir so left? Now I think / must closb, 'ant I shall write to you again du:lng the Ohristmas holidays. I wain, your loving nephew,
R. OLDKNOW.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you this fairy tale, and I hope you will be pleased with it. I am also sending you a riddle,- having read that you wanted some.
I remain, your loving niece,
JANE PASSMORE.

THE OLD MAN AND HIS GRANDSON. Once upon a time there was a very old, old man whose eyes were dim, his ears useless for hearing, and his knees trembled. When he sat at fable• he could scarcely hold his spoon, and often he spilled his food over the table-cloth and sometimes down his clothes. His son and daughter-in-law were much vexed about this; and at last they made the poor old man sit behind the oi;en in a corner, and gave him his meals in an earthen dish—and not enougil, either. The poor man grew sad, and his eyes were moistened with tears. Once his hands trembled so that he could not hold the dish, and it fell on the ground and broke all to pieces. The young wife scolded him, but he made no reply, and only sighed. After that, they bought him a wooden dish for a couple of pence, and out of that he had now to feed. One day, when he was sitting in his usual place, he saw his little grandson, four years•Q. old, upon the ground, fitting together pieces of wood. "What are you makiThri asked the old man. "I am making a wockder! trough," replied the child, "for .father and mother to feed out of w these words the man looked at his wife a little while, and presently when / grow big." At they began ta cry, tthheneiy, and let the old grandfather sit at always take his meals. there, nr tableec e wfaonirtdthh they did not even say anything if he , spilled a little on the table-cloth. They never more gave him the wooden dish to eat out of.

div.p: A RIDDLE.
There was a man of Adam's race, Who had a certain dwelling-place; Not in Heaven, nor earth, nor Hell, But where do you think that men did dwell t Answer: Jonah, in the whale's belly.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS=FASHION-HOME.
EMERALDS AGAIN' POPULAR.

Emeralds are again at the zenith of their popularity, and this is scarcely to be wondered at, since they are , probably the most becoming of all jewels, their k colour improving the appear- ance of almost any skin.. They share with dia- rconds the accusation of being cold, but there are many Who prefer their mysterious hints of far seas and haunted glades in deep forests, to the smouldering, winking fires of the mkt, which call to mind the tapping of the Nibelung s hammer and the red embers glearnitig Wotan's sword Nothung. As for pearls, they stand apart, in unquestioned supremacy.

div.head: Fnocx FOE A CHILD.
div.p: Fnocx FOE A CHILD.

Our sketch shewS :fro& of some useful-and becoming child's electric-131 U 0 woollen material, though l the colour is entirely a matter of choice. A pretty golden brown or the ever-useful navy serge would work out equally well. The bodice and skirt are made separately and joined at the waist. The rounded opening at the neck is out- lined with a strap of darker-toned velvet, which is arranged with little tabs on the shoulders fastened with dull silver buttons, the two ,tabs

in front being arranged to come over the two centre pleats. Instead of sleeves there are two cape-like frills, both edged with a narrow band of velvet. The sl:irt is pleated, the pleats being stitched to about half-way clown, or to meet the upturned points of the velvet strap that trims the skirt. To wear beneath this pinafore frock a short blouse will be needed. This could be of plain electric-blue silk, or white delaine pat- terned with a blue flower or spot. CLOTHES AND THE WOMAN.

- , I It is a sad reflection that with all our atten- tion to dress, our tremendous expenditure, our new 'fabrics and trimmings, and our crowding fashiOn . papers, we merely fritter, and do not achieve any really notable thing in the way of garments, says a writer in the Globe. A typical " creation " of the presant day consists of a flimsy material loaded with lace, embroidery, jewels, and other overlying matters. In perhaps one case out of a hundred the magnificence is designed to suit . the appearance of the wearer ; her eyes and her hair, her expression, her jewels, her gown, make up a connected whole; she herself is the visible meaning of it all. In the other ninety-nine cases, one beholds a Gown, a. Hat, and some Jewels. Further obser- vation reveals a woman, carefully arranged to ' suit her frock; one may truly say of her that " She is as pretty as a picture," since the is 60 much prettier than herself. Our modern idea of beauty is the smooth lack of character which one may study in any doll-shop. One is for ever meeting well-carried clothes; now and then one meets a well-dressed woman, and the beautiful completeness of her, the way in which her beauty of self is reflected and enhanced by the 1 --,, beauty of her garments, is a delight which on. prizes :n proportion to it.; rarity. The well- essed woman is easily recognised ; her eyes are first' and their meessatro is received before Sr clothes are noticed. Instead of thinking her zt Pretty as a picture come to life: one wiebea for a painter to perpetuate her living self ; she has not been inspired, but is inspiring. No ono has romantic thoughts about the well-carried clothes, nor wishes to find out what life has meant yes of , their to the expressionlem e wearers; whereas no one fails to wonder about and love the woman whose character is not eclipsed by ler dress, her own sex most of all. 41, AFTLANOON BLOUSE. Shown in our sketch is an afternoon blouse suitable for wearing with a tailor-made costume. It could be carried out in cashmere or soft satin, but would look smartest realised in chiffon taffetas,. in a pretty pale shade of old rose. Down the front of the blouse there is a stitched plastron, cut with three narrow tabs at each side; these cross over the two pleats on either

and fasten with a small velvet-covered but. , ton at the neck. The plastron is cut out in I long narrow oval and piped at the edges with deep old-rose velvet. Beneath, there is a dainty guimpe of Valenciennes lace, adorned with a row of velvet buttons, and a small bow at the • throat. The under-part of the sleeve has two small stitched tabs at the elbow, where the sleeve is finished with two frills of soft lace lawn.

div.head: JEux INNOCENTS.
div.p: JEux INNOCENTS.

Bridge is not the only amusement at our smart country-houses, writes "A Society Butter- fly "- in 31. A. p. Jeux innocents, as they are termed, make many a frolic between tea and dinner. At. a rec'ent week-end each guest was asked to write down what he or she ' thought were the best sources of happiness. To my thinking, health, .Wealth, and freedom coino first among "the things that matter." But one woman declared .that health, wealth, and youth were the most important. Personally. I think that the joys of extreme youth arc. often over- ..ated; at any rate, if one were again seventeen. t, would be good to have the experience of hirty. But we all wish to be young, and .many I us prolong our youth to a quite indefinite nod. The art of' beauty is studied with suc- in 1906.

div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
div.p: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
Lancashire Cup
WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
Fish's Arm Broken.

Saturday's final for the Lancashire Cup at Wigan was a memorable encounter. Warrington went to meet Broughton Rangets at Wigan with high hopes of success and were supported by quite 3,500 spectators from the good old town. All hopes were dashed to the ground in the first five minutes of the gome, for Fish, the Warrington captain and star threequarter, sustained a fracture of the right and the arst time ,he was tackled and of course took no further part in the game. The game was well contented after this an" Warrington did well to score 2 tries to 3 goals 3 tries by the Rangers. Perfect football weather favoured the contest and there was a crowd of 15,000 people on the Wigan Football Club's fine enclosure, toe gate money totalling, £392. Teams and officials : Broughton Bangers—Barton, back ; Hogg, Wilson, C. James, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; S. James and Flynn, half backs ; Beetham, Mottram, Darlison, Whitehead, Clampitt, and Ruddick, forwards. Warrington—Berry, back ; Fish, Dickinson, Taylor, and Brookes' three-quarter backs ; Lees and Hockenhall, half backs ; Boardman, Preston, Thomas, Naylor,Eleath, and Harmer, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes. Touch judges, Messrs. W. Jones, Runcorn, and C. Platt, Swinton. Having lost the toss, the Rangers 'Commenced the game, and Flynn getting the better of the ensuing punting exchanges,the play opened well in the Warring- ton half. Dickinson cleared cleverly by getting in a hugh kick, though surrounded by his opponents, which found touch at the half-way line. This was the pre- lude to a burst by Claude James, which ended in War- rington beinr, pinned on their own lines. A bout of passing by the Broughton backs looked dangerous, but Fish cleverly intercepted Wilson's pass to Hogg and dashed down the touch-line,with Lees close by. He only got about a dozen yards before being tackled quite fairly and then to the consternation of the crowd the Referee was seen leading Fish from the ground and supporting his right arm. A ,medical examination soon proved that the arm was badly fractured, and quite a damper was thrown on the prcceedings. Thomas took his captain's vacant place, and the Rangers still maintained the offensive. Only about one minute had elapsed from Fish's injury when Flynn dropped at goal, and the ball fell clearly a couple of feet uhder the bar. Referee Smith signalled a goal, and despite the protests of the Warrington men and the frantic shouts of the crowd at that end of the ground the point was allowed. This reverse only served to stimulate Warring- ton. Their forwards worked hard, but found the long raking kicks of Wilson a decided stumbling block. Berry was laid out in the charge of the Broughton forwards and while he was lying stunned Wilson got hold after a bad knock-on and rushed over the line with a try. There was no goal, but for a few minates War- rington had only eleven men Heath having to take Berry's place at full back till he revived. On the full back's return, Warrington put in some dashing work and Brooks created a sensation by beating Barlow for posses- sion near halfway and racing clear for the line. He appeared a certain scorer, but when there was only a yard to go Hogg come across and pulled him down on the line. It was a brilliant effort and deserved a better fate. Broughton were penalised soon after this and Preston had the hardest luck with a long shot for goal. Broughton attacked again, but the tackling of the Warrington men was capital and half time arrived with the score unaltered : Rangers, 5 points ; Warrington, nil.
- ton.

On resuming, Broughton led the first attack but were repulsed by Dickenson. The relief was only temporary and the Rangers backs bore down on the line with good passing and Hogg should have got an easy try but missed the final pass. Warrington could not get the ball away and in the scramble on the line Darlison got a lucky try for Broughton. Warrington again rallied pluckily, and Thomas broke through at half way. Dickenson got in front and spoiled a promising opening. Warrington had a short spell on the attack but were driven to the line again. where Harris smartly dropped a &,oal.The Rangers had all the play at this point and Berry being hard pressed tried to kick dead but merely sent the ball over his own line and Flynn raced up for an easy try, Again Warrington changed the venue by desperate forward work and the ball coming loose lathe Rangers quarters, Thomas picked up and threw to Hockenhall. The latter passed to Dickenson and after some pretty exchanges the cenre crossed the line with the best try of the day. Preston made a fine shot at goal but only hit the near upright. The Rangers made a brief visit the Warrington end again and Harris kicked a penalty goal. Warrington showed surprising determination and fine play by Lees and Taylor took the ball to tke Rangers' line where it only required touching down. Clampitt saved with a kick over the touch line. Warrington pressed home the advantage and getting the ball from the scrum Lees threw wide to Brooks who dashed over.nt a great pace, Preston failing to convert. Final Broughton Rangers, 3 goals 3 tries (15 points) ; Warrington 2 ties (6 points), PRESENTATION OF THE CUP.

After the match Mr. J. 11. Houghton, treasurer of the Lancashire Union, presented the cup to the Broughton Rangers captain, R. Wilson. . In doing so, Mr. Houghton expressed the regret of everyone present at the accident which had befallen Fish. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He was not prepared to say what the result of the game would have been if the Warrington csptain had taken part in the whole of the struggle. Nevertheless he congratulated the Rangers upon their success. (Cheers). Yorkshire Cup Final Bradford beat Hull Kiegston Rovers by 3 points to 5 at Wakefield before 10,000 people. Bradford got all their points in the first half and had the worst of the game later. The Rovers missed some ridiculously easy chances of scoring in the second half, and were unlucky to lose. div.head: PAPER FROM COTTON STALKS.
div.p: PAPER FROM COTTON STALKS.

The manufacture of paper from the fibre of the cotton-stalk is one of the latest inventions which .are said to have passed the experimental stage. It is asserted th—at all grades of paper, from the best form of linen to, the lowest grade, can be manufactured from cotton-stalks. In addition to this, a variety of by-products, such as alcohol, nitrogen, material for gun-cotton and smokeless powder can also be secured in paying quantities. Mills for the use of cotton-stalks in that way may become general in the cotton-growing States. If is estimated that on an area of land producing a bale of cotton at least one ton of stalks can be gathered. Upon this basis, froria 10.000,000 to 12.000,000 tons of raw material could be secured for the production of paper: which would in- crease the value of the cotton crop of the South- ern States nearly £2,000,000.,

ARE WE EVOLVING MORE BRAIN POWER? The recent rapid acceleration of .s'cientific pro- gress is a striking fact.. Whether it is due to in- creased power evolved in the human intellect mins considered at 'a British Association meeting. The opinion was expressed that it would -be a bold thing to assert that, the mind is more powerful than in the days of Homer, Pericles. and Archi- medes. The mystery may be explained by the extension ,of our senses by mechanical appliances. The bolometer and electric coherer have in- creased the range of our vision a thousand-fold; the electroscope and the galvanometer have ex- tended our sight and touch until we can detect an electron. By the many instruments supplying the deficiencies in ouk faculties we go forward confidently where previously all was dark.

div.head: LIFE HISTORY OF THE EEL.
div.p: THE LIFE HISTORY OF THE EEL.

The mystery which has so king shrouded cer- tain important facts in the life history of the eel are being gradually cleared up. It is now some time since a group of small-headed, transparent and ribbon-shaped fish, named by naturalists Leptocephalia, were identified as the young of various species of eel. Among these Italian naturalists recognised the one named Leptoceph- alus brevirostris as the young of the common eel. It was further determined that eels spawn in the Mediterranean in comparatively deep and warm water. The most recent information as to the spawning place of the eel is to be found in the journal of the Marine Biological Associa- tion. Drs. Schmidt and Petersen, of the Inter- national - Fisheries Investigation Association, have found quantities of Leptocephali," or young eels, in the depths of the Atlantic. They .conclude that eels spawn in deep and relatively warm water north-west and west of Scotland.
EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE ON RADIUM.

One of the most distinctive peculiarities of radio-active change as distinguished from chemical change, writes the Hon. R. J. Strutt, F.R.S., is its indifference to temperature. Chemical actions are, of course, very largely de- pendent on temperature conditions. Thus, for , example, all chemical actions with one exception —the combination of hydrogen with fluorine-- are suspended at the low temperature of liquid ' hydrogen. Again, chemical activity is usually very much stimulated by rise of temperature. Oxygen and hydrogen are, so far as is known, quite inert towards each other at ordinary tem- peratures. When the temperature is raised ex- plosive combination follows. On the other hand. radio-active change is very much less dependent on temperature. In the case of radio-activity we have a means of determining how fast the change is proceed- ing in the exterior electrical effects which the rays from the changing substance are capable of producing. Some experiments made at Man- chester seemed to shew that there was some slight influence of temperature. Further research cast considerable doubt on' the validity of this conclusion. A paper read before the Royal Society by Dr. Bronson describes experiments on the subject which gave a result altogether negative, although the temperature employed was considerably higher than in the former in- vestigation. Some radium was hermetically sealed in a tube made of quartz glass, which does not soften below a white heat. This was placed in a coil of wire which could be • electricaty heated, and its radio-activity was watched by means of its electrical discharging power at some distance off, due fo penetrating rays which were able to traverse the quartz tube. It was found that even after prolonged exposure to a full white lit-at the activity of the radium was in no degree affected. Nor did any change occur on cooling. This result is of great importance, for it emphasises more completely than ever the doctrine that radio-activity is in no way co- related with chemical change, but is of quite a different nature. It is also important in connec- tion with the modern theory of the earth's heat, as showing that even where the temperature is very high inside the earth the activity of radium is in no way suspended.

div.head: IS THE EARTH CONTRACTING?
div.p: IS THE EARTH CONTRACTING?

. - - Every educated person has been taught to be. lieve that the earth is a fiery mass surrounded i by a crust. This crust, it s further assumed, was formed by the gradual cooling of our planet. The cooling process continues still and results in a 'contraction of the earth. In time, accordingly, our planet' must become as cold, if not quite as small, as the moon now seems. All this. however, turns out to be a caricature of reality' in the light of the views recently ad- vanced in Nature on the authority of those eminent scientists, the lion. R. J. Strutt.F.R.S., and Dr. W. J. Gregory, Professor of Geology at the University of Glasgoiv. Professor Strutt asserts that it is highly unscientific to regard the heat Of the earth as merely a remnant of the heat generated by contraction of a primeval nebula. A few years ago it was suggested in the Recite 'Seiriitifique that there might be enough radium in the earth to account for the planet's internal heat. Professor Strutt says, I however, that he and his associates have ex• arnined a large number of rocks, both igneous 4 and sedimentary, and have been led to the con- clusion that there is very much more radium in all of them than would be needed to maintain the earth's internal heat if the earth were con- stituted of rock throughout. From this Pro- fessor Strutt concludes that the interior of the earth does not contain radium. Its composition is probably quite different in all respects from that of the surface materials of the globe. His data for the quantity of radium in rock point to a thickness of terrestrial crust of at least forty- five miles. Such a thickness of rocky crust would contain amply sufficient radium to main- tam the earth's effective temperature. Calcula- tion on these premises, on the assumption that the capacity of rock to conduct heat was not much affected by changes of temperature, proved that the internal temperature at the bottom of the terrestrial crust would be about I,soodeg. Centigrade. The real questien in dispute, howrver, accord- ing to Professor Gregory, is geological. The chemistry of radium emanations is incidental. As it presents itself to the geological mind, the problem is whether the high density of the earth's interior is due to conipression or to segre- gation. If the compression theory- the idea of contraction through cooling rhe accepted. the interior of the earth necessarily consists of the same material as the surface. If the segregation theory--which may be represented objectively nby a huge canon-ball, coinciding with the earth's interior, surrounded by a lighter coating of matter—be adopted, it does not necessarily follow that the earth cools and contracts. The suggestion that the earth is contracting by cool- ing is often erroneously attributed to geology. We derive it in reality from astronomy, and if the theory be exploded it is the outlook of the astronomers. As a geologist, Professor Gre- gory says he inclines to abandon the belief that the earth is contracting by cooling. The gene. , cal observations on displacements of rocks dc not. favour the theory of a contracting earth. It .is true that observation of some rock forms points to contraction, but it is not clear even then that such contraction is the result of cool- ing.. So much has called for explanation in the tight of discovery in recent years that the cool- rim hvnothesis has become inaclenuate. What nypotnesis should take its maw rrotessot Gregory would not venture to say, but it is at all events manifest to him that a fundamental proposition of the astronomers on the atthjeol 311 lb. earth is now exploded.

The Non-Traders would enlarge this barrier by extending it to interests which Councillors may have in limited companies. itself, it is node L. die, unnecessary to prevent suc“ _ investor from entering the Council. That is, supposing one of our late Mayors had £5O in such a firm as Pearson Knowles and Co., Ltd., any benefit that such might derive through the Council giving an order to such a firm would amount perhaps to an eighth of a ' penny. I think lam right In stating that the Non- ' Traders recognise that it would be absurd to contend ' that such a man would tamper with his honour for the sake of half a farthing. Where then are we to draw the line ? We have three factors to consider in making, either by statute or usage, a definite rule (and all such rules must be definite, or they are unworkable) first a man's means, second the proportion the shares bear , to the whole capital of which these shares form a part, and third the amount of the investment itself. At present the law recognises that as a rule a man's all, or at any rate his main interest, is in his own business,and , therefore, considering the danger imminent, bars all personal trading. But as a rule it is a man's sn.plus that is invested in shares in limited companies, the pro- portion of individual holdings is generally small as; compared with the whole, and therefore, since the I danger is not imminent the law has not been extended; to limited companies. lam well aware that there are exceptional cases, for example, a "one man company" I where the danger may be as imminent as in the case of a private firm. The law however must provide for the 1 rule, rather than the exception, and in my opinion, in I this case, it wisely stops short at individual traders. It I should be recognisdd that law, at the best, is a clumsy expedient, even the present law, good and wise as its intentions are, involves a town in possible loss. Its I representatives are debarred from trading with one of their number even although such a one could serve ' them better than any other, and should a citizen , be debarred from entering the Council I because of his investment, or shculd a Councillor resign to make the trading legal,the town loses services which may be of great value. This is the condition under the existing law. How much weightier would these disadvantages be if the Non-Trader's contention I were crystalized into law or usage. These disadvantages would become greater as time goes on. in an increasing extent commercial enter- prises are worked, not by individual capitalists, but by the co-partnership of many individuals, with their ' liability limited by the amount of their holdings. Indeed, in the not distant futdre, if the Non-Traders' ' contentions were carried out we should be faced with I one of two alternative. First, all business men who I invest their capital in local industrial undertakings would be prevented from serving the town ; or second,if such entered the Council much of the work would have to I go to companies or individuals outside the town,because of the investment of the Conncillers in local companies I would bar a participation of Warrington people in the' work required for the town. To erect a barrier which would prevent business men from taking part in the service of their town, would detract from the ability of the Council in the sphere of practical management of municipal undertakings, which are sure to increase, and for which a business career gives special knowledge and

training. I would invite the opinion of the people of Warrington on the general question. Surely it is worth while giving earnest and reasoned consideration to this matter, and surely it is not worth while dragging it into the mire by unworthy personalities. CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, sth December, 1906.

Sir,—l am glad to see from your last issue that Mr. Dodds has said his last word in the correspondence with Mr. Parker. He has failed so far to get any clear and distinct answer to the question he raised, and he would get nothing more if he continued the correspond- ence ad infinitum. Mr. Parker apparently does not want to answer the question as to the position of the Liberal party in the Non-Trading matter, and he is probably constitutionally compelled to wander round a point rather than go straight at it. It is just the same with the Latchford election ; much discourse, but nothing said. There are men who do not like finality. It is so interesting, when cornered, to drop the point at issue and start a moral discctr-e on another topic,which can be continued until the exasperated hearers grow tired and the protagonist can escape while the audience sleeps. Sir, we are very weary. Let Mr. Parker take the hint and vanish ere we wake.—Yours LIBRA v Warrington, December 7th, 190 G.

Pauper Labour. Sir,—My letter which appeared in the columns of your paper of the 2ith ult.,concerning the recent prose- cution of a pauper painter by the Board of Guardians has inspired a reply from Mr. Patrick O'Brien. You. Sir, were graciously pleased to add a footnote to my letter. In the first place. I would thank my friend Mr. O'Brien for so candidly admitting that he has read my letters from time to time" with interest and frequently with sympathetic appreciation "; he is afraid, however, that he " cannot endorse my sentiments on the above ' stbject." In the second place, I am pleased to observe he recognized the fact that Twasconcerned with principles and not with persons: that my letter was an expression of opinion and not an attack on individuals. I took the case as a sample, recognizing in it one of every-day occurrence. It appealed to me to be unfair, and I said so. I will now try to prove it. The pauper WRS a painter. It is customary, I believe, to strip the paper from the walls before putting on fresh paper ; and as, I presume, the walls in question were not different from other walls in that particular, the same process had to be adopted. That is to say, the unskilled labour had to preceed the skilled. Now, Sir, was the painter engaged to do the unskilled labour only or was he engaged to do the whole of the work—the unskilled and the skilled labour ? If he was engaged to do the unskilled labour only, why should the gentleman who appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Board of Guardians tell the magistrates, as is reported in the Press, that "after Clarke ceased to work, a tender was obtained for the work at .£l6. so that had he continued there was pleat,' of work to keep him busy for many weeks." The work of stripping the paper from the walls of one shop and one room of another would not, I think," have kept him busy for many weeks." Again, if he was engaged to do the stripping only— which work would probably find him employment for not more than a fortnight—what was to become of him when the two weeks were up? Was he to go back to the Workhouse and be prosecuted ? Or was he to be received with open arms because he had accomplished the " impossible" task of doing work in a fornight which ought to have kept him busy for many weeks ? Why was the man prosecuted? I have previously pointed out that during the time he had been in the Workhouse he had been very useful and had unques- tionably saved the ratepayers a large amount of money. The person who engaged him had no personal grudge against him as he, to use his own words, "had not sus- tained any loss or injury by the man leaving the work be was engaged on." Then, surely, the only mistake the man committed was in returning to the workhouse a week sooner than be ought to have done ! He com- mitted no crime—other than in choosing the inside in

div.head: MAYORAL "AT HOME." -- SUCCESSFUL FUNCTION.
div.p: MAYORAL "AT HOME." -- SUCCESSFUL FUNCTION.

The Mayor and Mayoress Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst) held an " At Home ' at the Town Hall on , Thursday afternoon, and the function proved highly successful. About a thousand townspeople attended ,to pay their respects to the Mayor and Mayoress, and throughout the afternoon there was a constant stream of visitors. The entrance hall presented a very pleasing and animated appearance, choice chrysan- themums and other plants having been tastefully arranged by Mr. R. Whitfield, the head gardener. , The visitors were received in the Council Chamber ! and were cordially welcomed by the genial chief I magistrate and his wife. The Mayoress was very becomingly attired in a black chiffon velvet Princess dress over heliotrope taffetas. The yoke was coin- posed of embroidered ivory chiffon edged with handsome lace Berthe of Brussels point. The , dress, which was generally admired, was ; made by the Misses Woods, of Rylands-street. ' Refreshments were served in the Committee Rooms, I the catering being in the hands of Mr. and Mrs. Powis. Mr. Alfred Starkey's band- was in attendance, and played a capital selection of music in an exceedingly creditable manner. The programme was as follows : Grand March "Festal " M. E. Dandridge. div.head: Services for Sunday.
div.p: Services for Sunday.

The annual choir festival will be observed at Bold-street Wesleyan Churchand will bathe occasion of the holding of special services at which the preacher will be the I Rev. Enoch Salt (Southport). Special music will be rendered both morning and evening, whilst in the after- noon the choir will give the cantata "A song of thanks- giving." Wycliffe Congregational Church: Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30, Rev. J. Yonge. Golborne-street Baptist Church: Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30, Pastor John Taylor. Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church : Preachers, 10. 30 Rev. E. J. Gawne ; 6.30, Rev. S. Pitt. Latchford Baptist Church : Preacher, Rev. J. F. Matthews. Subject 10.30, "A curious curiosity," and 6 o'clock, "The tragedy of a great life."

A railway accident, which fortunately resulted in no I one being injured, occurred at Helsby on Saturday, I shortly after twelve noon. It appears that alter the ten minut 39 past twelve passenger train from Hooton, which runs via Ellesmere Port to Helsby, had dis- charged its passengers at the latter station, whilst being shunted ran foul of a goods train on the main line from Chester. The engine of the empty passenger train was overturned, and the driver and fireman experienced a narrow escape of being seriously. injured. The damage to the goods train was only slight. The accident, happening at such a busy point, naturally caused con- siderable delay to the traffic. A breakdown gang from Chester were kept busy on Saturday and Seaday clearing the obstruction. FREE SPEECH AT WIDNES. CROWDS MENACE THE POLICE. The police-Salvation Army controversy took a decidedly serious turn on Saturday evening, when the police arrested Adjutant Carrot, of Manchester, after refusing to give his name and address. The meeting commenced in Vine-street at seven o'clock, and after the close of this the Army marched down Lugsdale-road to the big lamp in the square. Upon arrival at the prohibited spot they marched round and round whilst the service was in progress. Twenty ininutes later Inspector Blackburn, who was accom- panied by two sergeants, came from the police station. He walked round theaautskirts of the crowd for some time, then made his way into the centre, the crowd opening out to allow him to pass. At this juncture there was great hooting and booing on the part of the crowd, which, at the request of the Army leaders, were at once hushed. The inspector stepped on to the stone parapet round the lamp and spoke to Adjutant Carrol, who was in charge of the meeting. With him he con- tinued in conversation for some little time, when the officer demanded ' his name and address. The adjutant wished to know for what purpose, protesting at the time that he was causing no oestruction. The name and address were refused. The same request was made by the police officer to the remainder of the Army officerv, but in each case the reply was in the negative. A constable was hurriedly despatched to the _police station—presumably for reinforcements—but whilst he was away the time of service had expired, and the meet- ing was brought to a close.—Carrol was taken to the police station, followed by an angry crowd of almost 1,500 people, who with loud cries and yells hooted the I police, and made a hostile demonstration in front of the , police station. 'The Rev. Alexander Harvey, who had been a spectator on the fringe • of the crowd, walked down to the police station, with Inspector Blackburn, and requested permission to enter the office. Before doing so he made a strong , appeal to the crowd to desist from their hostility, and to quietly disperse. In the station the inspector again , demanded the names, which were at once forthcoming., He then turned to Superintendent Strickland and asked if he should also take the name of Colonel Wilson, the commander of the North West Province, to which the superintendent replied, " Certainly, if he was amongst them." Colonel Wilson. demanded to know why they wanted his name,' and protested that he had not been near the meeting, having only walked into the crowd in company with the inspector, and the reason he bad ' come to the police station was to offer bail, if neces- sary. The police officer then turned to the Rev. A. Harvey and raked for lais address, which, with a simile was given. The Army officers then left the police station, where they were greeted with loud cheers from the cr,)wd, and escorted to the railway station, where the police again received a very hostile demonstration.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON

DISTURBANCES AT EARLESTOWN. Kate Bradley, Jane isuckley, and Elizabeth Cawley were summoned at Newton on Thursday for using bad language and making a disturbance in Lord-street, Earlestown, late on the night of November 9th.—P.C. Mullen said he was called out of bed to quell a great disturbance, and found the three women shouting and swearing at each other.—Fined ss.each including costs. Robert Edwards, Albert Cooper, Robert Smith, Albert Durber, and William Walls were summoned for using bad language on November 9th, in Bridge-street, Earlestown.—lnspector Innes said their conduct was verg disgraceful. They had been previously cautioned.— Fined 2s. od, each and costs. Samuel Tickle summoned Richard Parkin for hitting him on the nose while he stood at his own door, in Houghton-street, on the night of November 10th:— Plaintiff said he was knocktu n own and had his ribs kicked, by this young man and others.—After several witnesses had been called on both sides to settle the question which side began the fighting, the case was dismissed. GAME TRESPASS AT NEWTON: At Newton Petty Sessions last week Roger Golding, who did not appear, was summoned for a game trespass in the day time on Mr. Alderson's farm, off Visto-road. —Mr. Arthur Brown, prosecuting for Lord Newton, said it was an easy thing for people living in Vista-road to get on to the adjacent land and back again to their houses. This man did not live there ; he lived a mile and a half away, but he borrowed a double-barrelled gun from a Vista-road resident, and was caught by two keepers in the middle of a clover field with both barrels of his gnu loaded and capped. He said he was going to shoot a rat, but as the keepers did not believe him he begged to be let off.—William Middleton and his son deposed that they were watching Robins Row and they caught the defendant as stated by Mr. Brown. Golding asked to be let off, but was told he had killed too much that field to be lot off.—Defenclant (who had reemne on tnvicted 9 times before) was fined 40s. and costs, and the Chairman, understanding that he had no gun licence, hoped the Excise would look into that. div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN DEWHURST.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN DEWHURST.
Forty Years Headmaster at Warrington.

It is with deep regret that we record the death at Southport on Tuesday evening of Mr. John Dewhurst who until recently was a prominent figure in local educational circles. The news came as a shock to most Warringtonians who were not even aware that Mr. Dewhurst was seriously ill. It is only a little over twelve months since he retired from the head- mastership of the Warrington Parochial Boys' School which he had occupied with distinction for over forty vearsand went to live at Southport a town to Which he was much attached. His numerous friends joined in wishing him that long retirement which he had so well earned by his devoted labours. It was only compara- tively recently that the state of,his health began to occasion anxiety. He suffered from an internal com- plaint despite every attention pissed away at the time stated.

An eminently Useful and successful scholastic career is thus brought to a close. Mr. Dewhurst, who was sixty-seven years of age, was a native of Whalley,near Blackburn. He was educated at the Higher Grade School, Dukinfield, where he served as a pupil teacher under the headmastership of Mr. Dowse, 8.A., and subsequently went to Culharn College, Oxford, for a two years' training. At the early age of twenty-two he came to Warrington in 1802 to take over the duties of schoolmaster at the Parish Church schools and choir master at the church. At that time the average school attendance was 150, whereas it is now about 700. The school was worked by the master and pupil teachers for ten years. Then a certificated assistant was appointed. Now the staff includes thirteen certificated class teachers. The pupil teachers from the parochial school have been very successful and many are now headmasters of important schools. The parochial school has gained the highest grants each year, and all the reports from numerous inspectors have testi- fied to the excellence of the teaching. Mr. Dewhurst took a prominent part in the formation of the Pupil Teachers' Central Classes, and acted as secretary and treasurer for eight years, until the classes were taken over by the Education Authority. In Church work he rendered active service during the whole of the period of his residence in Warrington, having , filled the important posts of choirmaster, sidesman, churchwarden and secretary of the Church Council of the Parish Church. The recent scheme for the restoration of the venerable church was one which he I had very much at heart. Mr. Dewhurst studied music under Dr. Hiles for five years, two for voice produc- tion and singing and three for organ playing. An enthusiastic sportsman, Mr. Dowhurst played for the Warrington Click-et Club for twenty years, and for several seasons was the highest scorer, his average working out at between 24 and 28 runs for the whole of the season. He figured with equal success as a bowler. As a manager of the Savings Bank for many years, Mr. Dewhurst had taken a deep interest in the welfare of the institution and had regularly attended I the annual meetings. When Mr. Dewhurst tendered his resignation of the headmastership of the Parochial School, the School I Management Committee voiced the general feeling of ithe townspeople in the following resolution :—" That I the Committee do place on record their high apprecia- tion of the long and valued services rendered by Mr. Dewhurst to the cause of education in the town, and do express their hope that he may be long spared to enjoy the rest he so well deserves."—Subsequently at a representative gathering of old scholars Mr. Dew- hurst was presented with a handsome silver tea service of Queen Anne design, and the headmasters of the town entertained him at a complimentary dinner. By all who came into contact with Mr. Dewhurst in a public or private capacity, his death will be very deeply regretted. As the holder of a responsible position he had exerted a great influence for good on the youth of the town and, thanks to his wise tuition, many of them have attained honourable offices in the commer- cial and municipal worlds.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral, which took place yesterday afternoon, was the occasion of a striking demonstration of respect for the deceased gentlemen. Prior to the interment a service was held at the Parish Church, there being a crowded congregation. As the mourners entared the Church" 0 rest in the Lord "was played by Mr. F. M. Darby, followed by" I know that my Redeemer liveth." The service was conducted by the Rector, assisted by I the Rev. W. Blakeney, rector of Moyle Brace, South- port. The chief mourners were :—Mr. J. C. Dewhurst, Dublin (son), Miss Dewhurst (daughter), Mr. H. Dewhurst (nephew), and Miss Dewhurst (niece), Bamber Bridge, Mr, Proger (brother-in-law), and Mr. D. Proger, jun., nephew.
