div.p: ST HELENS.
ANOMER NEW SCHOOL FOR ST. HELENS.

1, The Bt. Helens,Tosen Council have decided to ask for ' the permission of the Local Government Board to borrow £1,540 for tne purchase of a site between Denton's Green and Newtown,for the erection of u large school for those districts. ' SCHOLARS' EYESIGHT.

The St. Helens Education Committee have decided to distribute among the parents of the scholars attending the public elementary schools of the borough, cards giving information and advice as to the best means of preserving and safeguarding the eyesight of their chil- dren. NEW PAROCHIAL HALL AT ST. HELENS.

The vicar and parishioners of St. Mark's Church, Cowley Hill, have for some time bean endeavouring to secure a new parochial hall for the parish, and the vicar, Bev. T. W. Ketchlee, announces that Sir David Gamble has given a site for the hall in %Vinci le-street, and has promised to give £3OO to the building fund. Mr. and Mrs. Martin Elammill have given £lOO, the Bishop of Liverpool £25, and Miss Gamble £25. The hall is expectedto cost over .£3,000. ST. HELENS BETTING CASES.

Thirty-six summonses for street betting and assisting ! in the commission of this offence were down for hear- ing at St. Helens on Monday. Fourteen defendants were the subject of the summonses, viz.:—Albert , Pearce, 25, Barton-street (thiee cases); John Barnes, 38, Wilson-street (three charges) ; Michael Collins, 80, College-street (six summonses) ; William Anders' 1 101, Central-street (one case) ; John Anders (four cases); Bertha Anders (three cases) ; Moses Middlehurst, 157, 1 College-street (two cases); Joseph Mort, 39, Crab- , street, (three cases); James Thomas; 13, Oldfield-strcat , (three cases); George Chisholme, 45, Napier-street 1 (three cases) ; Albin Bond, Kiln-lace (one ease) ; IJoseph Bethel, 133, Wilson-street (one case) ; William Glynn, 121, Lyon-street ' • and Edward Brownbill, 92, Dunriding.—The Chief Constable said that the number of street bookmakers in St. Helens was being decreased. I—The total fines and costs amounted to £157 7s. which 1 considerably increases the sums drawn from the local ; bookmakers since July last years which previously ' amounted to £3BO. THE ST. HELENS SHOOTING CASE. At Liverpool Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Sutton, Isaac Arnold (28), hospital porter, and Ernest Worthington (21), gardener, pleaded guilty to having, at St. Helens, had housebreaking implements in their , ;possession at night on August 28. The two men were 1 discovered at midnight by Police Constable Smith in ' the grounds of the St. Anne's Bowling Club. Arnold heed a revolver twice, but he afterwards pleaded that he had no intention of harming the officer, and that he oily fired to frighten him. On the previous day he was I teed for shooting the constable with intent to murder , him, but the jury found him not guilty.—Mr. H. L. I Riley, who defended the two prisoners on the charge to I which they pleaded guilty, appealed to his lordship for a lenient sentence, having regard to the previous good character of the men. They had already been in gaol for three months.—The Judge said that he was deter- mined to protect the police in the execution of their duty. By his act Arnold might have caused the death of the policeman, or at any rate might have caused him grievous bodily harm. If the latter had been the case Arnold would certainly have had to go to penal servitude. He took into consideration the good character of the men, and under the circumstances he sentenced Arnold ; to twelvemonths' imprisonment and Worthington to six months' imprisonment.

div.head: GARDEN SUBURBS.
div.p: GARDEN SUBURBS.
MOVEMENT INAUGURATED AT WARRINGTON.
Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.

There is every prospect that in the near future War- rington will have a Garden City suburb. The move- ment was inaugurated at a mdeting convened by the Committee of the Beautiful Warrington Society and held at the Town Hall yesterday afterooon. Canon Morley Stevenson presided over a large attendance which included the Borough Member (Mr. A. H. Crosfleld) and Miss Crosfleld. The principal speaker was Mr. Crossley Greenwood, organizing secretary of the Co-partnership Tenants' Housing Council. The CHAIRMAN said that when they began to consider the desirability of making the town in which they lived as beautiful as they could, they were very soon brought face to face with the fact that unless they could catch up the building operations of the future, their work would be very largely undone. At the present moment the builder or builders placed their streets of little houses where they would and in what direction they would and in accordance with what laws of building they thought proper, and the consequence was that there were continually growing up upon the outskirts of our towns rows of streets which were not in con- formity with the laws of beauty. If the work of beautifying towns was to be accomplished it could only be by trying to capture the outlying districts and take measures to see that the building operations should be more in accordance with the ideals of the beautiful, of health, convenience and comfort. That seemed to be the root notion of a Garden City suburb. (Applause.) Mr. CROSSLEY GREENWOOD then delivered a very interesting address. At the outset he quoted some , striking figures showing that while the population of agricultural districts had been steadily decreasing the population a towns had been correspondingly increas- ing. They had to face the fact that England was a vast workshop and the consequence was that I land in towns had greatly increased in value. The wages of the working classes were based on the law of supply and demand and were mainly on a subsistence level. The result was that the most unskilled of the labourers had had to occupy dwellings which were cheaper and which had in many instances been made cheaper by crowding together as many houses as possible, Three and a quarter millions of our popula- tion were estimated by the Local Government Board to be living in overcrowded conditions and nearly 700,000 were living, eating, sleeping and dying in one room. It was a pressing necessity that something should be done to ameliorate those conditions. (Hear, hear.) The Garden City movement was a step in that direction. Mr. Greenwood then detailed what had been done at Letchworth where the Garden City Company were developing an estate. Three parishes had been bought and Joined together and at the outset the estate was carefully planned out and arrangements made as to drainage Scc. The result was that they were able to provide sufficient air space in the houses, as well as open spaces and playing grounds. He suggested that a similar movement should be inaugurated at War- rington by the formation of a company. (Applause.) There should be a fixed rate of interest on capital of 5 per cent. and any additional profits should be devoted to developing the estate. At the present time there were ten such societies with a capital of £125,081. Mr. Greenwood considered that workingmen would be only too willing to avail themselves of the opportunity of living under such surroundings and instanced how the promoters of one recently-formed estate had been inundated with applications for land. (Applause). Several questions were asked. In reply to Miss Crosfield, Mr. GREENWOOD said the usual rent charged was 6 per cent, on the cost of the house. If a house cost £2OO the rent would be ss. per week, exclusive of rates and taxes. Mr. H. R0131:11T8 moved a vote cif thanks to Mr. Greenwood. He said the tendency of public opinion and of legislation was in the direction of giving larger powers to progressive municipalities in regard to build- ing. In the meantime, however, they could not afford to stand still and see the errors of the past so fre- quently repeated. Therefore the adoption of such a scheme as Mr. Greenwood had described should be taken up as early as possible. (Applause.) Alderman BF.NNETT seconded and endorsed these views. It had been proved by practical experience that the idea of a Garden City could be carried out and Warrington ought to be in the forefront of such a movement. "Philanthropy at 5 per cent" was a fair description of the object they had in view. (applause.) The vote was heartily accorded. Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., moved a vote of thanks to the Beautiful Warrington Society for convening the meeting and to Canon Stevenson for presiding. He said that although, unfortunately, he (Mr.Crosfleld) had not been directly connected with the Beautiful War- rington Society he took a very keen interest in the pro- gress of the movement. If he remembered rightly, Macaulay in one of his essays dealt in a most scathing manner with the poet Southey who had been denounc- ing modern industrialism and its progress and the utilitarian side of it all, because it interfered with the picturesque aspect of the old dilapidated buildings and with cottages that were very insanitary but very quaint. (Laughter,) Certainly, in these modern times, with the immense extension of our big cities, we had all seen that utilitarianism bad been allowed to usurp the claims we owed to the artistic side of life. One saw it in all the towns, and, he was sorry to say, more particularly in the towns and cities of England. Per- haps we were less favoured in climate than some Con- tinental cities. But while we were proud to say that the standard of comfort and well-being on the whole was higher in England than in foreign countries' in point of beauty we bad to take second place. (Hear, bear.) He was not going to blow the trumpet of any particular firm in Warrington; lit would be very improper to do so. (Laughter.) He saw his old friend Alderman Bennett smiling. They knew a little bit about the old question of smoke and Other matters—(hear, hear,)—and they , had to combat these great evils in the cities and towns of Lancashire. It certainly was a work beyond all

praise when people would help to extend a 1 practical and feasible attempt to make things a little bit more beautiful and to bring what Matthew Arnold called " sweetnes and light "nearer to the homes of the poorer people in our towns. (Applause.) That commendable object was being carried out by the Beautiful Warrington Society to whose work the Chairman. had given a splendid. impetus for which they all owed him the greatesit thanks—(hear, hear)—and they were still more indebted to Canon Stevenson and to the Society for going a step forward and bringing the great scheme of Garden Cities before them in a practical manner in order,they hoped, that it might receive support from private people ' so far as they could afford and were inclined to support it, in advance of such improvements being undertaken by municipalities—which they hoped would certainly be the case in the near future. (Hear, hear). Prior to that they must look to individuals to give the lead to governing bodies, as they had done on so many other occasions, and if Warrington would be to the front in the case of Garden Cities as it fortunately was in the case of the Beautiful Warrington Society, they would give some return to Mr. Greenwood for his lecture and also encourage the men who were working tooth and nail to make the scheme of Garden Cities a practical success, to bring about its extension through England, and to interestas manyas possible of the mem-- 4 bers of the House of Commons in it. (Hear, hear). , would probably interest that gathering when he stated he supposed the most active man in the House in con- nection with the scheme was a gentleman who bad addressed Warrington audiences politically during tti: last twelve months—Mr. H. Vivian. (Applause. worked incessantly to bring about an extensionefthe scheme and he (Mr. Crosfield) was sure that h would movement. (Applause.) taking ienxgc exceedingly d that 11 Mrs. GATZNETT seconded and said a could —0 msee that Warrinon was in something in their respective localities to promote the y thatpl splendideasea to growth of the love of natural things. (Applause.) Mr. C. E. PARKER, who has been one of the pioneers of the scheme, moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor for the use of the. Council Chamber, and dealt with the financial aspect of the undertaking. They hoped, he said, to follow the lead of the Garden City and form two companies—the parent company, and secondly a scheme on co-operative lines for the working-classes. They had got a promise from Mr. Vivian to come to Warrington and address an evening .meeting on the question. The financial support already promised was sufficient to make a start, but he wanted the scheme to be a big one, and suggested that £lO,OOO would be desirable. Mr.W.Long had promised a substantial sum, and another gentleman was willing to put in a tenth of all that was raised ,up to £lO,OOO. They bad several other promises, and hoped there would be a good response from all who were interested. The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK seconded, and the vote was heartily accorded.

Mr. Crosfielcl is in full sympathy with all that tends towards improving the lot of the masses—as becomes .a democratic Liberal ALP, * * Our readers will be interested to hear that the foundation stone of the Infirmary extension will be laid on Thurs4y, January 31st by Lord Lilford. The subscription list has now reached the handsome ' total of £10,127 ISs. Id. * * * It is saddening to think that after so many years of active work, Mr. John Dewhurst lived such a short time to enjoy his well-earned retirement. Probably no man in Warrington had worked harder for educa- tion and a great number of "old boys" can testify to the value of the training which they received at his , hands. * * * Like the Beautiful Warrington Society, the Garden Suburb scheme seems to have caught on and has every prospect of being carried to a successful issue. Sufficient financial support has already been promised to set the thing fairly going and the desired capital of .elO,OOO appears to be by no means out of reach. Mr. Henry Vivian, M.P., .who is the leader of the national movement, is announced to visit Warrington shortly and expound its aims. Our readers will recollect that Mr. Vivian helped Mr. Crosfield during the elec- tion campaign and won great public favour as a speaker and worker in the cause of Labour.
